P2497.title: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit Bank 2
P2497.plain: A general circuit fault on the position feedback sensor of the EGR cooler bypass valve on bank 2. EGR mixes inert exhaust into intake to lower combustion peak temperature — too little raises NOx, too much causes misfires and rough running.

P2498.title: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Range or Performance Bank 2
P2498.plain: Same as P2493 on bank 2. EGR mixes inert exhaust into intake to lower combustion peak temperature — too little raises NOx, too much causes misfires and rough running.

P2499.title: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit Low Bank 2
P2499.plain: Same as P2494 on bank 2. EGR mixes inert exhaust into intake to lower combustion peak temperature — too little raises NOx, too much causes misfires and rough running.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P249A.title: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit High Bank 2
P249A.plain: Same as P2495 on bank 2. EGR mixes inert exhaust into intake to lower combustion peak temperature — too little raises NOx, too much causes misfires and rough running.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P249B.title: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent or Erratic Bank 2
P249B.plain: Same as P2496 on bank 2. EGR mixes inert exhaust into intake to lower combustion peak temperature — too little raises NOx, too much causes misfires and rough running.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P249C.title: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Reductant Injection Control
P249C.plain: After cold start the AdBlue injection runs open-loop until SCR temperature is reached. The transition into closed-loop is taking longer than calibrated.

P249D.title: Closed Loop Reductant Injection Control At Limit Flow Too Low
P249D.plain: With reductant injection running closed-loop the controller drives the dosing valve to maximum opening but cannot reach the required AdBlue flow.

P249E.title: Closed Loop Reductant Injection Control At Limit Flow Too High
P249E.plain: Same as P249D with the controller fully closing the dosing valve yet still measuring more flow than needed - the valve does not seat fully.
causes: Dosing valve does not seat fully

P249F.title: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Particulate Filter Regeneration Control
P249F.plain: The DPF regeneration controller cannot transition into its closed-loop temperature control quickly enough - typically because EGT does not rise to setpoint within the calibrated window.

P24A0.title: Closed Loop Particulate Filter Regeneration Control At Limit Temperature Too Low
P24A0.plain: With regeneration running closed-loop the controller is at maximum heat-input demand yet cannot raise EGT to setpoint - typical for a load-poor drive cycle.

P24A1.title: Closed Loop Particulate Filter Regeneration Control At Limit Temperature Too High
P24A1.plain: Same as P24A0 with the controller fully reducing heat input yet EGT still rising - typical for a runaway exotherm in the DPF (oil contamination).

P24A2.title: Particulate Filter Regeneration Incomplete Bank 1
P24A2.plain: Particulate Filter Regeneration Incomplete Bank 1: the control module has detected this fault condition.

P24A3.title: Particulate Filter Restriction Soot Accumulation Bank 2
P24A3.plain: The DPF on bank 2 has accumulated soot beyond the normal operating window. Active regeneration will be requested.

P24A4.title: Particulate Filter Restriction Soot Accumulation Too High Bank 1
P24A4.plain: Particulate Filter Restriction Soot Accumulation Too High Bank 1: the control module has detected this fault condition.

P24A5.title: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Stuck Open Bank 1
P24A5.plain: The EGR cooler bypass valve on bank 1 is mechanically stuck in the open (bypassing) position - EGR always bypasses the cooler, gas reaches the intake hotter than designed.
causes: Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play

P24A6.title: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Stuck Open Bank 2
P24A6.plain: The EGR cooler bypass valve on bank 2 is mechanically stuck in the open (bypassing) position - EGR always bypasses the cooler, gas reaches the intake hotter than designed.
causes: Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play

P24A7.title: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Control Circuit Open
P24A7.plain: The dedicated coolant pump for the EGR cooler has an open control circuit - the pump cannot run, EGR cooler temperature rises beyond the safety threshold.
causes: Pin pushed back out of connector body
Cracked solder joint inside the module or sensor

P24A8.title: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Performance Stuck Off
P24A8.plain: The pump is electrically intact but does not deliver flow when commanded - typically a worn impeller or seized rotor.
causes: Pump impeller worn or rotor seized
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play

P24A9.title: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Control Circuit Low
P24A9.plain: Same as P24A7 with the control line shorted to ground. EGR mixes inert exhaust into intake to lower combustion peak temperature — too little raises NOx, too much causes misfires and rough running.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24AA.title: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Control Circuit High
P24AA.plain: Same as P24A7 with the control line shorted to supply. EGR mixes inert exhaust into intake to lower combustion peak temperature — too little raises NOx, too much causes misfires and rough running.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P24AB.title: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Stuck On
P24AB.plain: The pump or its driver is stuck on - the pump runs continuously, even with the engine off, draining battery and bleeding heat from the engine.
causes: Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play

P24AC.title: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Feedback Circuit Low
P24AC.plain: The feedback line that confirms pump speed reads below the plausible range - either pump not turning or feedback line shorted to ground.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24AD.title: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Feedback Circuit High
P24AD.plain: Same as P24AC with the feedback line shorted to supply. EGR mixes inert exhaust into intake to lower combustion peak temperature — too little raises NOx, too much causes misfires and rough running.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P24AE.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Circuit
P24AE.plain: A general circuit fault on the particulate matter (PM) sensor - measures soot in the exhaust downstream of the DPF to verify regeneration.

P24AF.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Circuit Range or Performance
P24AF.plain: Same as P24AE with the signal in plausible range yet not matching the engine model.

P24B0.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Circuit Low
P24B0.plain: Same as P24AE with the signal voltage below the plausible range. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24B1.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Circuit High
P24B1.plain: Same as P24AE with the signal voltage above the plausible range. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P24B2.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Circuit Intermittent
P24B2.plain: Same as P24AE with intermittent or erratic signal. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P24B3.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Heater Control Circuit Open
P24B3.plain: The PM sensor heater (regenerates the sensor by burning off accumulated soot) has an open control circuit.
causes: Pin pushed back out of connector body
Cracked solder joint inside the module or sensor

P24B4.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Heater Control Circuit Range or Performance
P24B4.plain: Same as P24B3 with the heater control loop in plausible range yet not matching the heater model. The sensor heater warms the element to operating temperature (~600 °C); without it the lambda sensor stays inactive in closed loop and the ECM cannot trim mixture.

P24B5.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Heater Control Circuit Low
P24B5.plain: Same as P24B3 with the control line shorted to ground. The sensor heater warms the element to operating temperature (~600 °C); without it the lambda sensor stays inactive in closed loop and the ECM cannot trim mixture.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24B6.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Heater Control Circuit High
P24B6.plain: Same as P24B3 with the control line shorted to supply. The sensor heater warms the element to operating temperature (~600 °C); without it the lambda sensor stays inactive in closed loop and the ECM cannot trim mixture.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P24B7.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Heater Resistance
P24B7.plain: The resistance of the PM sensor heater is outside the calibrated band.

P24B8.title: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Pressure Sensor Circuit
P24B8.plain: A general circuit fault on the LDP internal pressure sensor. The evaporative system captures fuel vapor from the tank and purges it into intake; leaks or stuck purge valves leak hydrocarbons and cause emissions failures.

P24B9.title: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Pressure Sensor Circuit Range or Performance
P24B9.plain: Same as P24B8 with the signal in plausible range yet not matching the pump operating curve. The evaporative system captures fuel vapor from the tank and purges it into intake; leaks or stuck purge valves leak hydrocarbons and cause emissions failures.

P24BA.title: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P24BA.plain: Same as P24B8 with the signal voltage below the plausible range. The evaporative system captures fuel vapor from the tank and purges it into intake; leaks or stuck purge valves leak hydrocarbons and cause emissions failures.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24BB.title: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Pressure Sensor Circuit High

causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P24BD.title: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Switching Valve Control Circuit Open
P24BD.plain: The switching valve in the LDP - directs pump output between EVAP test path and reference orifice - has an open control circuit.
causes: Pin pushed back out of connector body
Cracked solder joint inside the module or sensor

P24BE.title: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Switching Valve Control Circuit Low

P24BF.title: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Switching Valve Control Circuit High
P24BF.plain: Same as P24BD with the control line shorted to supply. The evaporative system captures fuel vapor from the tank and purges it into intake; leaks or stuck purge valves leak hydrocarbons and cause emissions failures.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24C0.title: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Switching Valve Stuck On
P24C0.plain: The LDP switching valve is stuck in the activated position. The evaporative system captures fuel vapor from the tank and purges it into intake; leaks or stuck purge valves leak hydrocarbons and cause emissions failures.
causes: Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play

P24C1.title: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Switching Valve Performance Stuck Off
P24C1.plain: Same as P24C0 with the valve stuck off. The evaporative system captures fuel vapor from the tank and purges it into intake; leaks or stuck purge valves leak hydrocarbons and cause emissions failures.
causes: Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play

P24C2.title: Exhaust Gas Temperature Measurement System Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 1
P24C2.plain: The multiple EGT sensors on bank 1 disagree by more than the diagnostic tolerance under stable conditions - one of them has drifted relative to the others.

P24C3.title: Exhaust Gas Temperature Measurement System Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 2
P24C3.plain: The multiple EGT sensors on bank 2 disagree by more than the diagnostic tolerance under stable conditions - one of them has drifted relative to the others.

P24C4.title: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Exceeded Learning Limit Bank 1
P24C4.plain: The bypass valve position sensor learning has reached its software-side limit on bank 1 - typically heavy soot deposits have shifted the mechanical zero beyond the design adaptation range.
causes: Heavy carbon build-up on valve seat

P24C5.title: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Exceeded Learning Limit Bank 2
P24C5.plain: The bypass valve position sensor learning has reached its software-side limit on bank 2 - typically heavy soot deposits have shifted the mechanical zero beyond the design adaptation range.
causes: Heavy carbon build-up on valve seat

P24C6.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Temperature Circuit
P24C6.plain: A general circuit fault on the temperature element of the PM sensor - used to verify that the sensor is hot enough for measurement after regeneration.

P24C7.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Temperature Circuit Range or Performance
P24C7.plain: Same as P24C6 with the signal in plausible range yet not matching the engine model.

P24C8.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Temperature Circuit Low
P24C8.plain: Same as P24C6 with the signal voltage below the plausible range. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.

P24C9.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Temperature Circuit High

causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24CA.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Temperature Circuit Intermittent
P24CA.plain: Same as P24C6 with intermittent or erratic signal. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P24CB.title: Reductant Tank Cap Switch Circuit
P24CB.plain: A general circuit fault on the AdBlue tank cap switch - reports whether the cap is properly closed.

P24CC.title: Reductant Tank Cap Switch Circuit Range or Performance
P24CC.plain: Same as P24CB with input in plausible range yet not matching driver action.

P24CD.title: Reductant Tank Cap Switch Circuit Low
P24CD.plain: Same as P24CB with the signal shorted to ground. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24CE.title: Reductant Tank Cap Switch Circuit High
P24CE.plain: Same as P24CB with the signal shorted to supply. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24CF.title: Reductant Tank Cap Switch Circuit Intermittent or Erratic
P24CF.plain: Same as P24CB with intermittent or erratic signal. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P24D0.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit Low
P24D0.plain: The PM sensor supply voltage is below the plausible range. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24D1.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Regeneration Incomplete
P24D1.plain: A sensor regeneration cycle (heating to burn off accumulated soot) did not complete - sensor cannot return to measurement mode.

P24D2.title: Reductant Heater A Sense Circuit
P24D2.plain: Reductant Heater A Sense Circuit: an electrical fault is present in the circuit. The reductant (DEF/AdBlue) heater keeps the urea fluid from freezing; a fault can impair SCR dosing in cold conditions.

P24D3.title: Reductant Heater B Sense Circuit
P24D3.plain: Reductant Heater B Sense Circuit: an electrical fault is present in the circuit. The reductant (DEF/AdBlue) heater keeps the urea fluid from freezing; a fault can impair SCR dosing in cold conditions.

P24D4.title: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Feedback Circuit
P24D4.plain: A general circuit fault on the feedback line that the EGR cooler coolant pump reports speed on. EGR mixes inert exhaust into intake to lower combustion peak temperature — too little raises NOx, too much causes misfires and rough running.

P24D5.title: EVAP System Pressure Sensor or Switch B Circuit
P24D5.plain: A general circuit fault on the secondary EVAP system pressure sensor or switch B. The evaporative system captures fuel vapor from the tank and purges it into intake; leaks or stuck purge valves leak hydrocarbons and cause emissions failures.

P24D6.title: EVAP System Pressure Sensor or Switch B Circuit Range or Performance
P24D6.plain: Same as P24D5 with the signal in plausible range yet not matching the engine model. The evaporative system captures fuel vapor from the tank and purges it into intake; leaks or stuck purge valves leak hydrocarbons and cause emissions failures.

P24D7.title: EVAP System Pressure Sensor or Switch B Circuit Low
P24D7.plain: Same as P24D5 with the signal voltage below the plausible range. The evaporative system captures fuel vapor from the tank and purges it into intake; leaks or stuck purge valves leak hydrocarbons and cause emissions failures.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24D8.title: EVAP System Pressure Sensor or Switch B Circuit High
P24D8.plain: Same as P24D5 with the signal voltage above the plausible range. The evaporative system captures fuel vapor from the tank and purges it into intake; leaks or stuck purge valves leak hydrocarbons and cause emissions failures.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24D9.title: EVAP System Pressure Sensor or Switch B Circuit Intermittent
P24D9.plain: Same as P24D5 with intermittent or erratic signal. The evaporative system captures fuel vapor from the tank and purges it into intake; leaks or stuck purge valves leak hydrocarbons and cause emissions failures.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P24DA.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Exhaust Sample Error Bank 1
P24DA.plain: The PM sensor on bank 1 cannot acquire a valid exhaust sample - probe fouled, exhaust path obstructed at sensor, or sensor seal leaking.

P24DB.title: Reductant Purge Control Valve B Circuit Open
P24DB.plain: The secondary reductant purge valve B - which clears AdBlue from injector and lines at shutdown to prevent crystallisation - has an open control circuit.
causes: Pin pushed back out of connector body
Cracked solder joint inside the module or sensor

P24DC.title: Reductant Purge Control Valve B Performance
P24DC.plain: Same as P24DB with the actuator electrically intact yet not delivering the commanded purge flow. The evaporative system captures fuel vapor from the tank and purges it into intake; leaks or stuck purge valves leak hydrocarbons and cause emissions failures.

P24DD.title: Reductant Purge Control Valve B Circuit Low
P24DD.plain: Same as P24DB with the control line shorted to ground. The evaporative system captures fuel vapor from the tank and purges it into intake; leaks or stuck purge valves leak hydrocarbons and cause emissions failures.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24DE.title: Reductant Purge Control Valve B Circuit High
P24DE.plain: Same as P24DB with the control line shorted to supply. The evaporative system captures fuel vapor from the tank and purges it into intake; leaks or stuck purge valves leak hydrocarbons and cause emissions failures.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P24DF.title: Reductant Purge Control Valve B Stuck Open
P24DF.plain: Purge valve B is mechanically stuck open - AdBlue lines drain continuously, dosing pressure cannot build.
causes: Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play

P24E0.title: Reductant Purge Control Valve B Stuck Closed
P24E0.plain: Same as P24DF with valve B stuck closed - AdBlue cannot be cleared at shutdown, risk of crystallisation in injector and lines.
causes: Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play

P24E1.title: NH3 Sensor Circuit
P24E1.plain: A general circuit fault on the NH3 (ammonia) sensor - measures ammonia slip downstream of the SCR catalyst to detect AdBlue overdose.

P24E2.title: NH3 Sensor Circuit Range or Performance
P24E2.plain: Same as P24E1 with the signal in plausible range yet not matching the engine model.

P24E3.title: NH3 Sensor Circuit Low
P24E3.plain: Same as P24E1 with the signal voltage below the plausible range. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24E4.title: NH3 Sensor Circuit High
P24E4.plain: Same as P24E1 with the signal voltage above the plausible range. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P24E5.title: NH3 Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P24E5.plain: The ammonia (NH3) slip sensor downstream of the SCR catalyst delivers an intermittent or erratic signal. The ECM expects a smooth voltage proportional to ammonia concentration in the tailpipe — sudden jumps, dropouts or noise mean the wiring, connector or sensing element is failing. Used to close-loop the AdBlue/DEF dosing strategy.
causes: Chafed or vibrating harness near the exhaust
Aged ceramic sensor element drifting under heat cycles

P24E6.title: NH3 Sensor Heater Circuit/Open
P24E6.plain: The heater inside the ammonia (NH3) slip sensor warms the sensing cell to operating temperature so it can read tailpipe ammonia. The ECM detects an open in the heater control circuit — no current flows when the heater should be active, so the sensor never reaches its working point and SCR closed-loop control is suspended.
causes: Burnt-out heater winding inside the sensor
Failed heater driver stage in the dosing module

P24E7.title: NH3 Sensor Heater Circuit Low
P24E7.plain: The heater control circuit of the ammonia (NH3) slip sensor reads below the expected voltage range. Either the wiring is shorted to ground or the heater driver in the SCR/dosing module is stuck low. The sensor element never warms up, NH3 readings stay invalid and the SCR strategy falls back to open-loop dosing.
causes: Heater control wire shorted to ground
Internal short across the heater element
Low-side driver pulled down in the control module

P24E8.title: NH3 Sensor Heater Circuit High
P24E8.plain: The heater control circuit of the NH3 slip sensor reads above the expected voltage range. Typically a short to battery voltage or a heater driver stuck high — duty-cycle control is lost, the heater either runs continuously or not at all, and the sensor element risks overheating before the ECM disables it.
causes: Heater control wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24E9.title: NH3 Sensor Heater Circuit Performance
P24E9.plain: The heater of the NH3 slip sensor is electrically intact, but the warm-up profile or steady-state temperature feedback does not match the ECM model. The sensor takes too long to reach operating temperature or drifts away from setpoint, so SCR closed-loop control is delayed or held off.
causes: Poor thermal contact between heater and sensing cell

P24EA.title: NH3 Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit
P24EA.plain: The supply rail that powers the NH3 slip sensor electronics (typically 5 V or 12 V from the dosing/SCR module) is out of tolerance. Without a stable supply the sensor cannot deliver a valid ammonia reading, and the ECM disables the closed-loop SCR strategy.
causes: Failing supply rail inside the dosing module

P24EB.title: NH3 Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit Low
P24EB.plain: The NH3 slip sensor supply voltage drops below the lower limit. Usually a partial short to ground in the supply line, an undersized ground path with high resistance, or an internal supply collapse in the SCR/dosing module. Sensor output is held invalid until the supply recovers.
causes: High-resistance ground at the SCR module
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24EC.title: NH3 Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit High
P24EC.plain: The NH3 slip sensor supply voltage rises above the upper limit. Either the supply is shorted to battery voltage or an internal regulator in the dosing module has failed open. The sensor electronics may be damaged if the condition persists, so the ECM disables the input.
causes: Supply line shorted to battery voltage
Failed voltage regulator in the dosing module
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24ED.title: NH3 Sensor Calibration Memory
P24ED.plain: The NH3 slip sensor stores its individual calibration coefficients in non-volatile memory (EEPROM/flash). The ECM cannot read valid calibration values — either checksum fails, the memory is empty after replacement, or communication with the sensor electronics is broken. Without the trim values the raw ammonia reading is unreliable.
causes: New sensor installed but not coded/learned to the ECM
Corrupted calibration memory after voltage drop
Module software outdated, reflash may resolve

P24EE.title: NH3 Sensor Processor Performance
P24EE.plain: The microcontroller inside the smart NH3 slip sensor reports an internal performance fault — failed self-test, watchdog reset, or out-of-range plausibility checks. The sensor cannot guarantee its output value, the ECM marks the channel invalid and disables SCR closed-loop control on this branch.
causes: Module software outdated, reflash may resolve

P24EF.title: Control Module Wake-up Circuit/Open
P24EF.plain: The wake-up line that brings a sleeping ECU back from low-power mode is open. Many networks use a dedicated hardware wake-up wire (door-latch trigger, terminal 15, CAN wake-up) so modules can stay asleep with the ignition off. Without it, the module either fails to wake up at start-up or stays awake and drains the battery.
causes: Broken wake-up wire or unplugged connector
Failed wake-up input stage in the module
Pin pushed back out of connector body

P24F0.title: Control Module Wake-up Circuit Low
P24F0.plain: The wake-up input on the control module reads stuck low — usually a short to ground or a permanently asserted wake signal. The module either keeps waking up unnecessarily and drains the battery, or it cannot distinguish a real wake event from the stuck low level.
causes: Door, hood or terminal switch stuck closed
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24F1.title: Control Module Wake-up Circuit High
P24F1.plain: The wake-up input reads above the expected range — typically a short to battery voltage. The module sees a permanent wake-up request, never enters sleep mode and drains the battery while parked.
causes: Wake-up wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P24F2.title: EGR Temperature/Charge Air Cooler Temperature Correlation
P24F2.plain: After a long key-off soak both the EGR temperature sensor and the charge-air cooler outlet temperature sensor must read approximately the same ambient temperature. The ECM compares them and detects an implausible delta. One of the sensors drifts, is wired wrong, or is exposed to a heat source the model does not know about.
causes: Residual heat in the charge-air cooler after a hot soak

P24F3.title: Reductant Tank Temperature/Fuel Temperature Correlation
P24F3.plain: After a long key-off soak the AdBlue/DEF tank temperature and the fuel tank temperature should read close to each other (both at ambient). The ECM detects an implausible spread, which usually means one of the two sensors drifts, is wired wrong, or has a heat source nearby that the plausibility model does not account for.
causes: One temperature sensor drifting outside tolerance
Recently active reductant tank heater warming the tank above ambient

P24F4.title: NOx Sensor Delayed Response - High to Low Bank 1 Sensor 1
P24F4.plain: The pre-catalyst NOx sensor on bank 1 (sensor 1) reacts too slowly when NOx in the exhaust drops from a high to a low level — for example after a fuel cut or transition into low-load. Aged ceramic cells, soot deposits or condensation inside the sensor protective tube slow the diffusion of NOx to the measuring element.
causes: Aged sensor element with reduced response speed

P24F5.title: NOx Sensor Delayed Response - High to Low Bank 1 Sensor 2
P24F5.plain: The post-catalyst NOx sensor on bank 1 (sensor 2) reacts too slowly when NOx in the exhaust drops from a high to a low level. Same failure mechanism as the upstream sensor — aged element, soot or condensate — but post-catalyst the consequence is a degraded SCR conversion-efficiency monitor.
causes: Aged sensor element with reduced response speed

P24F6.title: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Stuck Open
P24F6.plain: On systems that inject HC dosing fuel or AIR-assisted reductant into the aftertreatment, a purge valve clears the line after each dosing event. The ECM detects the valve stuck open — pressure or flow does not build up against a closed valve, so the dosing line cannot be charged. Common on diesel HC-doser hardware (DPF regen support).
causes: Mechanically stuck open valve from soot or coking
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement

P24F7.title: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Stuck Closed
P24F7.plain: The aftertreatment HC dosing or reductant purge valve is stuck closed. The ECM commands purge but the line is not cleared, leaving residual fluid that can foul nozzles or freeze in cold weather. Subsequent dosing events also fail because backpressure does not match the model.
causes: Stuck closed by deposits or seized armature
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement

P24F8.title: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Control Circuit
P24F8.plain: General electrical fault in the control circuit of the aftertreatment fuel/air purge valve. The ECM cannot drive the valve coil according to plausibility checks — open, short or unexpected feedback voltage. Until cleared, dosing line purge is suspended.
causes: Failed driver stage in the dosing module

P24F9.title: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Control Circuit Range/Performance
P24F9.plain: The valve coil is electrically intact, but the response (current rise time, return-current decay, position feedback) does not match the ECM model. Typical for solenoids losing magnetic strength after long thermal cycling, or armatures with increased friction from coking.
causes: Aged solenoid with weakened magnetic force
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P24FA.title: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Control Circuit Low
P24FA.plain: The control circuit of the aftertreatment purge valve reads stuck low — usually a short to ground or a failed low-side driver. The valve is energised continuously when it should be off, or the diagnostic feedback voltage is pulled below threshold.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24FB.title: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Control Circuit High
P24FB.plain: The control circuit of the aftertreatment purge valve reads stuck high — typically a short to battery voltage or an open ground/return path. The driver cannot pull the line low to actuate the valve.
causes: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P24FC.title: Particulate Matter Sensor Heater Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P24FC.plain: The PM (soot) sensor heater is driven by a current-limited stage so it can burn off accumulated soot before each measurement. The driver reports current or junction temperature above the safe limit and disables itself. Often a partial short across the heater or sensor element after coolant intrusion.
causes: Partial short across the heater element
Driver overheating due to poor cooling on the module

P24FD.title: Particulate Filter A Incorrect
P24FD.plain: The ECM identifies the installed particulate filter A as the wrong part — backpressure signature, regeneration efficiency or coded part-number do not match the application. Common after a non-OEM aftermarket DPF or a wrong-application replacement.

P24FE.title: SCR Catalyst Incorrect
P24FE.plain: The ECM identifies the installed SCR catalyst as the wrong part — NOx conversion efficiency, NH3 storage capacity or coded part-number do not match the expected application. Typical after fitting a non-OEM SCR brick or after a coding error following replacement.
causes: Incorrect or non-OEM SCR catalyst installed

P24FF.title: Reductant Temperature Too High
P24FF.plain: The temperature of the AdBlue/DEF in the dosing system exceeds the safe limit — risk of thermal decomposition (NH3/biuret formation) and clogged dosing nozzles. Often caused by a stuck-on tank heater, a stalled coolant return or proximity to a hot exhaust component.
causes: Heat soak from exhaust or engine bay

P2500.title: Generator Lamp/L-Terminal Circuit Low
P2500.plain: The L-terminal feedback line from the alternator (charging warning lamp circuit) reads below the lower limit. The lamp may stay on, and battery voltage may drift if regulation feedback is also affected.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2501.title: Generator Lamp/L-Terminal Circuit High
P2501.plain: The L-terminal feedback from the alternator reads above the upper limit — short to supply or open ground side. Charging diagnostics cannot run cleanly.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2502.title: Charging System Voltage
P2502.plain: The ECU detects an out-of-range charging system voltage without specifying high or low. Indicates a generic charging fault that requires further sub-code investigation.

P2503.title: Charging System Voltage Low
P2503.plain: The ECU detects that battery voltage during operation stays below the regulated target. The alternator output is insufficient to maintain charge under load, eventually leading to battery depletion.

P2504.title: Charging System Voltage High
P2504.plain: The ECU detects a battery voltage above the regulated upper limit. The voltage regulator is not limiting alternator output, risking damage to electronic modules and battery overcharge.

P2505.title: ECM/PCM Power Input Signal
P2505.plain: The ECM/PCM monitors the main switched battery feed (typically terminal 15 / ignition-switched supply via the main relay). A general fault is reported — either the input is missing entirely or it does not match the expected timing relative to ignition state. Engine may not start or stay running.
causes: Blown fuse on the ECM power feed
Corroded connector pin at the ECM

P2506.title: ECM/PCM Power Input Signal Range/Performance
P2506.plain: The switched-battery input to the ECM/PCM is present, but the level or transient behaviour is out of plausibility — sagging during cranking, slow ramp-up after main-relay close, or noisy. Often caused by aged main relay contacts or a weak battery feed under load.
causes: Aged main relay contacts with rising contact resistance
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2507.title: ECM/PCM Power Input Signal Low
P2507.plain: The ECM/PCM switched-battery input reads below threshold while the ignition is on. Either the main relay does not close, the supply wire is broken or shorted to ground, or the battery is too low. Engine usually fails to start until the input recovers.
causes: Main relay does not pull in

P2508.title: ECM/PCM Power Input Signal High
P2508.plain: The ECM/PCM switched-battery input reads above the upper threshold. Most often caused by a charging system overvoltage (failed alternator regulator) or wrong jump-start procedure. Sustained high voltage risks damaging ECU electronics.
causes: Improper external power source or jump-start

P2509.title: ECM/PCM Power Input Signal Intermittent
P2509.plain: The ECU detects sporadic interruptions of its supply voltage. The fault is set when supply drops below a threshold for short periods, often during cranking or due to a poor connection.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P250A.title: Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit
P250A.plain: General electrical fault on the engine oil level sensor circuit. The ECM cannot read a plausible level signal (analog level, ultrasonic or capacitive sender). Without a valid level reading the ECM disables oil-low warnings and dynamic service-interval calculation.
causes: Open or shorted wiring to the sensor
Corroded connector at the oil pan

P250B.title: Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P250B.plain: The oil level sensor is electrically intact, but the level reading is implausible — for example a constant value across drives, jumps that cannot match real oil consumption, or readings outside the design range. Often a contaminated or aged float/ultrasonic sender.
causes: Foaming oil under high RPM masking the level
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P250C.title: Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit Low
P250C.plain: The oil level sensor signal voltage reads below the lower limit, typically a short to ground or an open at the reference end of the sender. The ECM treats the input as invalid and ignores oil-low warnings until the circuit is repaired.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P250D.title: Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit High
P250D.plain: The oil level sensor signal voltage reads above the upper limit, typically a short to reference voltage or an open signal return. Pegged at maximum, the ECM cannot distinguish full from invalid and disables the level monitor.
causes: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P250E.title: Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P250E.plain: The oil level signal jumps or drops out intermittently — usually loose contacts, vibration cracks at the sender or oil sloshing on bumpy roads. The ECM filters short transients but flags the input when the noise pattern exceeds the diagnostic limits.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P250F.title: Engine Oil Level Too Low
P250F.plain: The oil level monitor reports the engine oil level below the safe minimum after sensor checks pass. Continued operation risks bearing damage and oil-pump cavitation, so the ECM sets a critical warning, may reduce torque and asks the driver to add oil immediately.

P2510.title: ECM/PCM Power Relay Sense Circuit Range/Performance
P2510.plain: The voltage reported on the main power relay sense line for the engine controller does not match expectation. The ECU may shut down too early or stay awake too long, draining the battery.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2511.title: ECM/PCM Power Relay Sense Circuit Intermittent
P2511.plain: The sense (feedback) line that lets the ECM verify the main power relay has actually closed shows intermittent dropouts. The ECM expects to see battery voltage on this line whenever the relay is energised — short losses suggest aged contacts, vibration or chafed wiring.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P2512.title: Event Data Recorder Request Circuit/Open
P2512.plain: The Event Data Recorder (EDR / black box) request line — used by the ECM or restraint module to trigger the EDR to capture pre-crash data — is open. The ECM cannot trigger an event capture, so any subsequent crash event would not be recorded reliably.
causes: Open request wire or unplugged module
Failed input stage in the EDR
Pin pushed back out of connector body

P2513.title: Event Data Recorder Request Circuit Low
P2513.plain: The EDR request line reads stuck low — typically a short to ground or a permanently asserted request. The ECM either sees a constant request (which it cannot service) or cannot pulse the line high to fire a real event capture.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2514.title: Event Data Recorder Request Circuit High
P2514.plain: The EDR request line reads stuck high — typically a short to battery voltage. The ECM cannot pulse the line back low to release the request, so the EDR may either ignore further requests or sit in a permanent triggered state.
causes: Request wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P2515.title: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor B Circuit
P2515.plain: General electrical fault in the second A/C refrigerant pressure sensor circuit. Sensor B usually monitors the low-side or compressor-suction pressure (in addition to high-side sensor A). The ECM cannot read a plausible value and disables variable compressor control to avoid evaporator freeze-up or overpressure.
causes: Open or shorted wiring to the sensor

P2516.title: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P2516.plain: A/C refrigerant pressure sensor B is electrically intact, but its reading does not match the system model — for example pressures that do not fall when the compressor is off, do not change with ambient temperature, or contradict pressure sensor A. Often a refrigerant charge issue or a contaminated sensor.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2517.title: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low
P2517.plain: A/C refrigerant pressure sensor B signal voltage reads below the lower limit. Either a short to ground in the signal wire, an open reference voltage at the sensor, or an internal short. The ECM ignores the reading and disables A/C closed-loop control until the circuit recovers.
causes: Missing 5 V reference at the sensor
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2518.title: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor B Circuit High
P2518.plain: A/C refrigerant pressure sensor B signal voltage reads above the upper limit. Typically a short to reference voltage in the signal line, an open signal return, or an overpressure event briefly pegging the sensor. ECM disables variable compressor control to protect the system.
causes: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
Open signal return at the sensor
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2519.title: A/C Request A Circuit
P2519.plain: General electrical fault on the A/C compressor request input A. This input tells the ECM that the HVAC controller wants the A/C compressor engaged. With the input invalid, the ECM cannot enable the compressor clutch — A/C does not cool, idle-up compensation is not applied.
causes: Open or shorted A/C request wire
HVAC module not transmitting the request

P251A.title: PTO Enable Switch Circuit/Open
P251A.plain: The Power Take-Off (PTO) enable switch input to the ECM is open. PTO is used on trucks and work vehicles to drive auxiliary equipment from the engine — without a valid enable signal the ECM refuses to enter PTO operating mode, idle speed control changes do not apply.
causes: Open switch wire or unplugged switch
Pin pushed back out of connector body

P251B.title: PTO Enable Switch Circuit Low
P251B.plain: The PTO enable switch input reads stuck low — typically a short to ground or a permanently closed switch. The ECM either sees PTO enabled when the operator has not requested it, or cannot release the PTO mode after work.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P251C.title: PTO Enable Switch Circuit High
P251C.plain: The PTO enable switch input reads stuck high — typically a short to battery voltage. The ECM cannot pull the input low, so the switch state is unreadable and PTO mode is locked out for safety.
causes: Switch wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P251D.title: PTO Engine Shutdown Circuit/Open
P251D.plain: The PTO engine-shutdown command line is open. This safety input lets a connected work attachment (or operator switch) request an immediate engine shutdown — for example when an interlock is opened on a stationary aerial work platform. With the line broken, the safety shutdown cannot be commanded.
causes: Broken shutdown wire or unplugged work attachment
Pin pushed back out of connector body
Cracked solder joint inside the module or sensor

P251E.title: PTO Engine Shutdown Circuit Low
P251E.plain: The PTO engine-shutdown command line reads stuck low — usually a short to ground or a permanently asserted shutdown request. The ECM may treat this as an active shutdown command and refuse to start or keep the engine running while in PTO mode.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P251F.title: PTO Engine Shutdown Circuit High
P251F.plain: The PTO engine-shutdown command line reads stuck high — typically a short to battery voltage. The ECM cannot pulse the line low to acknowledge a shutdown request, so the operator-side safety chain is effectively disabled.
causes: Shutdown wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P2520.title: A/C Request A Circuit Low
P2520.plain: The A/C compressor request input A reads stuck low — typically a short to ground or a permanently asserted request. The ECM either sees A/C demanded all the time (cannot release idle-up, raises fuel use) or cannot distinguish a real request from the stuck low level.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2521.title: A/C Request A Circuit High
P2521.plain: The A/C request input A reads stuck high — typically a short to battery voltage. The ECM cannot pull the line low to read switch state, so the A/C compressor request is treated as invalid and the clutch stays disengaged.
causes: Request wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P2522.title: A/C Request B Circuit
P2522.plain: General electrical fault on the second A/C request input B. Many vehicles have two HVAC zones, a rear evaporator request, or a redundant request line — input B carries that signal. With the input invalid, the ECM cannot honour zone B compressor demand or rear-evap operation.
causes: Open or shorted A/C request wire B
HVAC module not transmitting request B

P2523.title: A/C Request B Circuit Low
P2523.plain: The A/C request input B reads stuck low — short to ground or permanently asserted request. Same effect as input A stuck low, applied to the second HVAC channel.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2524.title: A/C Request B Circuit High
P2524.plain: The A/C request input B reads stuck high — typically a short to battery voltage. The ECM cannot read the switch state, request B is treated as invalid.
causes: Request wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P2525.title: Vacuum Reservoir Pressure Sensor Circuit
P2525.plain: General electrical fault on the vacuum reservoir pressure sensor circuit. The reservoir stores manifold or pump-generated vacuum for systems like brake booster, EGR actuators or HVAC dampers. Without a valid reading the ECM disables vacuum-pump duty cycle control.
causes: Open or shorted wiring to the sensor

P2526.title: Vacuum Reservoir Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2526.plain: The vacuum reservoir pressure sensor is electrically intact, but the reading does not match the model — vacuum that does not build up after pump activation, does not bleed off when consumers draw, or stays at one value. Often a partly clogged hose, a leaking reservoir or an aged sensor.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2527.title: Vacuum Reservoir Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P2527.plain: Sensor signal voltage below the lower limit — usually a short to ground or open reference. The ECM disables vacuum pump control until the input recovers.
causes: Missing 5 V reference at the sensor
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2528.title: Vacuum Reservoir Pressure Sensor Circuit High
P2528.plain: Sensor signal voltage above the upper limit — usually a short to reference voltage or open signal return. ECM disables vacuum pump control to avoid overshooting.
causes: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2529.title: Vacuum Reservoir Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent
P2529.plain: The sensor signal jumps or drops out intermittently — loose connector, vibration, or chafed harness. The ECM filters short transients but flags the input when noise exceeds limits.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P252A.title: Engine Oil Quality Sensor Circuit
P252A.plain: General electrical fault on the engine oil quality sensor — typically a capacitive/dielectric sensor that estimates oil aging from permittivity, viscosity proxies and conductivity. With no valid reading the dynamic service-interval algorithm falls back to the fixed-interval default.
causes: Open or shorted wiring to the sensor
Failed sensor electrode after long use

P252B.title: Engine Oil Quality Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P252B.plain: The oil quality sensor is electrically intact, but the readings do not match the model — for example permittivity that does not change after an oil change, or shifts inconsistent with km/h driven. Often a contaminated electrode or oil that does not fit the sensor calibration.
causes: Oil grade outside the sensor calibration range
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P252C.title: Engine Oil Quality Sensor Circuit Low
P252C.plain: Sensor signal voltage below the lower limit — typically a short to ground in the signal line or an internal short across the sensor electrode.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P252D.title: Engine Oil Quality Sensor Circuit High
P252D.plain: Sensor signal voltage above the upper limit — typically a short to reference voltage or an open signal return.
causes: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P252E.title: Engine Oil Quality Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P252E.plain: The oil quality sensor signal jumps or drops out — usually a loose connector at the oil pan, an oil-soaked harness or vibration cracks at the sensor housing.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P252F.title: Engine Oil Level Too High
P252F.plain: The oil level monitor reports the engine oil level above the safe maximum after sensor checks pass. Overfilling raises foaming, blow-by and crankcase pressure — and on diesels with regen-by-injection, fuel dilution can drive the level up by itself. The ECM warns the driver and may flag for service.
causes: Fuel dilution from incomplete DPF regeneration

P2530.title: Ignition Switch Run Position Circuit
P2530.plain: The ECU detects an electrical fault on the ignition switch run position input. The signal indicating that the ignition is in the run position is missing or implausible.

P2531.title: Ignition Switch Run Position Circuit Low
P2531.plain: The ignition switch Run-position input reads stuck low — short to ground or a permanently closed contact. The ECM cannot tell when the operator releases the switch from Run, so accessory and crank logic gets confused.
causes: Run input wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2532.title: Ignition Switch Run Position Circuit High
P2532.plain: The ignition switch Run-position input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage or open switch return. The ECM cannot detect when the operator turns the switch back to off/accessory, so module sleep and accessory power timeouts do not work correctly.
causes: Run input wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P2533.title: Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit
P2533.plain: General electrical fault on the ignition switch On/Start (terminal 50 / crank) input. The ECM uses this signal to know when the starter is energised — without it the ECM cannot raise fuel and timing for cranking, the engine struggles to start or stalls right after.

P2534.title: Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit Low
P2534.plain: The On/Start input reads stuck low — short to ground or permanently closed contact. The ECM may see crank request when the key is at rest, blocking accessory functions or causing unexpected starter cut-off logic.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2535.title: Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit High
P2535.plain: The On/Start input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage. The ECM cannot read the crank state, modules dependent on this signal are unable to time their wake-up correctly.
causes: On/Start wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P2536.title: Ignition Switch Accessory Position Circuit
P2536.plain: General electrical fault on the ignition switch accessory (terminal 75 / ACC) input. ACC tells the ECM that radio, fans, accessory loads should be powered without the engine running. With the input invalid, the body controller may misjudge accessory power timing.

P2537.title: Ignition Switch Accessory Position Circuit Low
P2537.plain: The ACC input reads stuck low — short to ground or permanently closed contact. The ECM may see ACC active continuously and refuse to enter sleep, draining the battery.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2538.title: Ignition Switch Accessory Position Circuit High
P2538.plain: The ACC input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage. The ECM cannot detect when the operator releases the switch from ACC, accessory power timeouts do not work.
causes: ACC wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P2539.title: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit
P2539.plain: General electrical fault on the low-pressure fuel system sensor — typically the lift-pump or pre-supply pressure sensor that monitors the rail feeding the high-pressure pump. With no valid reading, the ECM cannot verify that lift pressure is sufficient for HP-pump intake.
causes: Open or shorted wiring to the sensor

P253A.title: PTO Sense Circuit/Open
P253A.plain: The PTO sense (engagement feedback) line is open. This input tells the ECM whether the PTO clutch or driveline is actually engaged after a request — it closes the loop on the PTO enable command. With it broken, the ECM cannot confirm engagement and refuses to ramp up to PTO speed setpoints.
causes: Pin pushed back out of connector body
Cracked solder joint inside the module or sensor

P253B.title: PTO Sense Circuit Range/Performance
P253B.plain: The PTO sense circuit is electrically intact, but the engagement feedback does not match the command. The ECM requests engage and sees no engaged feedback (or vice versa) within the expected time window — drive-line slip, sticky clutch, or a mis-adjusted limit switch.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P253C.title: PTO Sense Circuit Low
P253C.plain: The PTO sense input reads stuck low — short to ground or limit switch stuck closed. The ECM may see PTO continuously engaged.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P253D.title: PTO Sense Circuit High
P253D.plain: The PTO sense input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage or open switch return. The ECM cannot detect engagement.
causes: Sense wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P253E.title: PTO Sense Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P253E.plain: The PTO sense signal jumps or drops out — usually loose connectors, a chattering limit switch, or vibration on the work attachment.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P253F.title: Engine Oil Deteriorated
P253F.plain: The oil quality monitor concludes that the engine oil has reached the end of its useful life — based on permittivity, soot content, fuel dilution and total operating hours. The ECM requests an oil change before the next regen cycle to prevent accelerated bearing wear.
causes: High DPF regeneration load with fuel dilution

P2540.title: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit
P2540.plain: The ECU detects a general fault in the low-pressure fuel system pressure sensor circuit. Without a valid signal the ECU cannot verify lift-pump pressure or fuel rail pre-pressure.

P2541.title: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2541.plain: The signal of the low-pressure fuel sensor does not match the expected value during operation. Pressure does not rise as expected when the lift pump is commanded.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2542.title: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit High
P2542.plain: The low-pressure fuel system sensor signal voltage is above the upper limit. Either a short to reference voltage in the signal line, an open signal return, or a sensor reading pegged high after an internal failure. The HP-pump pressure-control strategy falls back to default.
causes: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2543.title: Power Demand Signal Circuit
P2543.plain: The ECU detects an electrical fault on the power demand input signal used to coordinate accessory loads (e.g. AC compressor, alternator load). The signal is missing or implausible.

P2544.title: Torque Management Request Input Signal A
P2544.plain: The ECU detects an invalid torque-management request signal A from another control unit (e.g. transmission, ESP, ABS) on the CAN bus. Cooperative torque control cannot be performed as expected.

P2545.title: Torque Management Request Input Signal A Range/Performance
P2545.plain: The ECM receives torque-management requests from other modules (TCM during shifts, ABS/ESC during traction events, hybrid controller). Input A is electrically intact but its values do not match the system model — out-of-range steps, jumps, or persistent values that other modules cannot confirm.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2546.title: Torque Management Request Input Signal A Low
P2546.plain: Torque management input A reads stuck low — analog short to ground or message stuck at minimum value. The ECM cannot trust the request and falls back to a safe default.
causes: CAN message stuck at minimum value

P2547.title: Torque Management Request Input Signal A High
P2547.plain: Torque management input A reads stuck high — analog short to reference voltage or message stuck at maximum value. The ECM rejects the request to avoid running unintended high-torque commands.
causes: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
CAN message stuck at maximum value

P2548.title: Torque Management Request Input Signal B
P2548.plain: General electrical fault on the second torque-management request input B. Used when more than one module needs to request torque adjustments — typically TCM on input A and ABS/ESC on input B, or chassis vs powertrain. With B invalid, only the A-side request is honoured.
causes: Open or shorted wire / invalid CAN message

P2549.title: Torque Management Request Input Signal B Range/Performance
P2549.plain: Input B is electrically intact but the values are implausible — same failure mode as the A-side performance fault, applied to the second torque-management channel.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P254A.title: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 1 Circuit/Open
P254A.plain: The PTO speed-selector switch 1 input is open. This switch lets the operator pick a preset PTO operating speed (idle, 800, 1200 rpm, etc.). With the input broken, the ECM cannot apply any operator-selected speed and falls back to a default speed.
causes: Pin pushed back out of connector body
Cracked solder joint inside the module or sensor

P254B.title: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 1 Range/Performance
P254B.plain: The selector input is electrically intact but the value is implausible — multiple positions asserted at once, or a value that cannot map to any of the configured speed presets. Often a sticky multi-position switch or a contaminated rotary contact.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P254C.title: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 1 Circuit Low
P254C.plain: PTO speed selector 1 input reads stuck low — short to ground or analog signal pegged at minimum. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P254D.title: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 1 Circuit High
P254D.plain: PTO speed selector 1 input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage or analog signal pegged at maximum.
causes: Switch wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P254E.title: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 1 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P254E.plain: The PTO speed selector signal jumps or drops out — usually a worn rotary contact or vibration on the work attachment.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P254F.title: Engine Hood Switch Circuit
P254F.plain: General electrical fault on the engine hood (bonnet) switch circuit. The hood switch tells the body controller and (on hybrids) the high-voltage system that the hood is open — used for security, alarm and HV-safety interlock. With the input invalid, alarm logic and HV interlock fall back to a safe state.

P2550.title: Torque Management Request Input Signal B Low
P2550.plain: Torque management input B reads stuck low — short to ground or message at minimum. ECM rejects the request, only A-side is used.

P2551.title: Torque Management Request Input Signal B High
P2551.plain: Torque management input B reads stuck high — short to reference voltage or message at maximum. ECM rejects the request to avoid unintended high-torque commands.
causes: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage

P2552.title: Throttle/Fuel Inhibit A Circuit
P2552.plain: General electrical fault on the throttle/fuel inhibit input A. This input lets external safety functions (immobilizer, hybrid HV interlock, anti-theft) override the throttle or cut fuel delivery. With the input invalid the safety override is unreliable, so the ECM falls back to its safe default — typically inhibit asserted to err on the side of safety.

P2553.title: Throttle/Fuel Inhibit A Circuit Range/Performance
P2553.plain: The throttle/fuel inhibit A signal is electrically intact but its value does not match the system context — for example asserted while the immobilizer reports OK, or de-asserted while a hybrid HV interlock is active. The ECM cannot trust the signal.
causes: Requesting module sending an inconsistent value
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2554.title: Throttle/Fuel Inhibit A Circuit Low
P2554.plain: Throttle/fuel inhibit A reads stuck low — short to ground or permanently asserted. ECM may treat it as continuous inhibit and refuse normal operation.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2555.title: Throttle/Fuel Inhibit A Circuit High
P2555.plain: Throttle/fuel inhibit A reads stuck high — short to battery voltage. ECM cannot read the inhibit state and falls back to the safe default.
causes: Inhibit wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P2556.title: Engine Coolant Level Sensor/Switch Circuit
P2556.plain: General electrical fault on the engine coolant level sensor/switch circuit. Many vehicles use a simple float-switch in the expansion tank, others use a continuous-level analog sensor. With the input invalid the ECM cannot warn for low coolant before overheating starts.
causes: Open or shorted wiring to the sensor
Corroded connector at the expansion tank

P2557.title: Engine Coolant Level Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance
P2557.plain: The coolant level sensor is electrically intact, but the readings are implausible — for example a level that does not move at all over many drive cycles, or jumps that cannot match real coolant loss. Often a stuck float, contaminated electrode or air-locked sensor.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2558.title: Engine Coolant Level Sensor/Switch Circuit Low
P2558.plain: Coolant level sensor signal voltage below the lower limit — short to ground or internal short. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2559.title: Engine Coolant Level Sensor/Switch Circuit High
P2559.plain: Coolant level sensor signal voltage above the upper limit — short to reference voltage or open signal return.
causes: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P255A.title: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 2 Circuit/Open
P255A.plain: The second PTO speed-selector switch input is open. Switch 2 typically encodes a binary or multi-bit code together with switch 1 — together they select one of several preset PTO speeds. With switch 2 broken, only the half of the bit pattern is available, so several presets cannot be reached.
causes: Pin pushed back out of connector body
Cracked solder joint inside the module or sensor

P255B.title: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 2 Range/Performance
P255B.plain: PTO speed selector switch 2 is electrically intact but its value does not match a valid bit pattern — multiple positions asserted, or values that do not map to any preset.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P255C.title: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 2 Circuit Low
P255C.plain: PTO speed selector 2 input reads stuck low — short to ground or analog signal pegged at minimum. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P255D.title: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 2 Circuit High
P255D.plain: PTO speed selector 2 input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage or analog signal pegged at maximum.
causes: Switch wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P255E.title: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 2 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P255E.plain: PTO speed selector 2 signal jumps or drops out — usually a worn rotary contact or vibration on the work attachment.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P255F.title: A/C Request A Circuit Range/Performance
P255F.plain: The A/C request input A is electrically intact, but its value does not match the system context — for example asserted while the HVAC controller reports off, toggling rapidly, or sustained while compressor pressures cannot support it. The ECM disables A/C clutch engagement until the input becomes plausible.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2560.title: Engine Coolant Level Low
P2560.plain: The coolant level monitor reports the engine coolant below the safe minimum after sensor checks pass. Continued operation risks overheating, head warping and head-gasket failure. The driver is warned and the ECM may reduce engine power until the level is restored.
causes: External coolant leak (hose, radiator, water pump)
Head gasket leaking coolant into combustion

P2561.title: A/C Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
P2561.plain: The A/C / HVAC control module has requested the ECM to illuminate the malfunction indicator (MIL) because of an emissions-relevant fault on its side. The original fault is stored in the HVAC module — this code only signals that the ECM has honoured the request.
causes: Internal fault in the HVAC module — read its DTCs

P2562.title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Circuit
P2562.plain: General electrical fault on the turbocharger boost control position sensor A — the feedback sensor on the wastegate or VGT actuator (often a contactless Hall sensor). Without valid position feedback the ECM cannot close the loop on boost control and falls back to open-loop duty cycle.
causes: Open or shorted wiring to the position sensor
Failed Hall element after thermal cycling

P2563.title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor Circuit
P2563.plain: The position feedback sensor on the variable-geometry or wastegate turbocharger actuator is not communicating or is implausible. Without position feedback, boost control runs in default mode and power is reduced.
causes: Wiring open or chafed near turbo

P2564.title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Circuit Low
P2564.plain: Position sensor A signal voltage below the lower limit — short to ground in the signal line or open reference voltage at the sensor.
causes: Missing 5 V reference at the sensor
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2565.title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Circuit High
P2565.plain: Position sensor A signal voltage above the upper limit — short to reference voltage in the signal line or open signal return.
causes: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2566.title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor Range/Performance
P2566.plain: The turbocharger actuator position sensor reports a value, but it does not track commanded vane or wastegate position within tolerance. Often a sticky VTG mechanism due to soot.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2567.title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor Circuit Low
P2567.plain: The turbocharger position sensor signal is below the lower limit — short to ground or sensor at zero stop.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2568.title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor Circuit High
P2568.plain: The turbocharger position sensor signal is above the upper limit — short to supply, open ground or sensor failed high.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2569.title: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P2569.plain: Direct Ozone Reduction (DOR) catalysts are coated radiator surfaces or dedicated catalysts that decompose tropospheric ozone passing over the radiator — used for low-emissions vehicles. The temperature sensor monitoring the DOR brick reads stuck low — short to ground or sensor short.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P256A.title: Engine Idle Speed Selector Sensor/Switch Circuit/Open
P256A.plain: The idle-speed selector input is open. On commercial vehicles this switch lets the operator pick a fast-idle setpoint (for example to keep auxiliary loads supplied). With the input broken, the ECM cannot apply an operator-selected idle speed.
causes: Pin pushed back out of connector body
Cracked solder joint inside the module or sensor

P256B.title: Engine Idle Speed Selector Sensor/Switch Range/Performance
P256B.plain: The idle-speed selector input is electrically intact but the value does not match a valid preset — multiple positions or a non-mappable value. Often a sticky multi-position switch.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P256C.title: Engine Idle Speed Selector Sensor/Switch Circuit Low
P256C.plain: Idle-speed selector input reads stuck low — short to ground or analog signal at minimum. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P256D.title: Engine Idle Speed Selector Sensor/Switch Circuit High
P256D.plain: Idle-speed selector input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage or analog signal at maximum. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Switch wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P256E.title: Engine Idle Speed Selector Sensor/Switch Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P256E.plain: The idle-speed selector signal jumps or drops out — usually a worn rotary contact or vibration. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P256F.title: A/C Request B Circuit Range/Performance
P256F.plain: A/C request input B is electrically intact but its value does not match the system context — same failure mode as the input A performance fault, applied to the second HVAC channel.
causes: HVAC module sending inconsistent request B
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2570.title: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Temperature Sensor Circuit High
P2570.plain: The DOR catalyst temperature sensor reads stuck high — short to reference voltage or open signal return. Without a valid temperature the ECM cannot enable the DOR efficiency monitor.
causes: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2571.title: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2571.plain: The DOR catalyst temperature sensor signal jumps or drops out — typically loose connectors or chafed wiring near the radiator pack.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P2572.title: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Deterioration Sensor Circuit
P2572.plain: General electrical fault on the DOR catalyst deterioration sensor circuit. This sensor estimates the remaining ozone-conversion capacity of the DOR coating — coating worn off the radiator surface, contaminated by salt or grime, or thermally aged. Without a valid signal the deterioration monitor is disabled.

P2573.title: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Deterioration Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2573.plain: The DOR deterioration sensor is electrically intact but its readings drift or do not match the model — for example a deterioration value that does not move with km/h driven, or moves implausibly fast.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2574.title: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Deterioration Sensor Circuit Low
P2574.plain: The DOR deterioration sensor signal voltage reads below the lower limit — short to ground or internal short.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2575.title: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Deterioration Sensor Circuit High
P2575.plain: The DOR deterioration sensor signal voltage reads above the upper limit — short to reference voltage or open signal return.
causes: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P2576.title: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Deterioration Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2576.plain: The DOR deterioration sensor signal jumps or drops out — typically loose connectors or chafed wiring near the radiator.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P2577.title: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold
P2577.plain: The DOR catalyst no longer reduces tropospheric ozone with the required efficiency, based on the deterioration sensor and operating-time model. Coating worn off the radiator surface, contaminated by road salt and grime, or thermally aged after many heat cycles. Replacing the affected radiator/coating restores function.
causes: DOR coating worn off the radiator
Coating contaminated by salt and grime

P2578.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Speed Sensor A Circuit
P2578.plain: General electrical fault on the turbocharger/supercharger shaft speed sensor A — a high-frequency Hall or eddy-current sensor on the compressor shaft. The ECM uses turbo speed for overspeed protection (typically 200,000+ rpm) and for closed-loop boost on VGT systems. With no valid speed the ECM limits boost.
causes: Aged sensor with reduced output amplitude

P2579.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Speed Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P2579.plain: Turbo speed sensor A is electrically intact, but the speed reading does not match the model — for example a speed that does not climb when boost rises, drifts away from the air-mass-flow estimate, or jumps. Often blade-fouling, a contaminated sensor tip or aged element.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P257A.title: Vacuum Reservoir Control Circuit/Open
P257A.plain: The control circuit that drives the vacuum reservoir control valve (or vacuum pump motor) is open. The ECM cannot energise the actuator, so vacuum is no longer maintained on demand and consumers like brake booster, EGR or HVAC dampers may run out of vacuum.
causes: Failed driver in the control module
Pin pushed back out of connector body

P257B.title: Vacuum Reservoir Control Circuit Low
P257B.plain: The vacuum reservoir control circuit reads stuck low — short to ground or low-side driver stuck on. The actuator may be energised continuously when it should be off.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P257C.title: Vacuum Reservoir Control Circuit High
P257C.plain: The vacuum reservoir control circuit reads stuck high — short to battery voltage or open coil. The driver cannot pull the line low to actuate the valve/motor.
causes: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
