Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P257D.title: Engine Hood Switch Circuit Range/Performance
P257D.plain: The hood switch is electrically intact, but its state is implausible — for example reporting hood-open while vehicle speed is rising, or rapid toggles. Usually a worn switch with high contact bounce or a misaligned hood actuator.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P257E.title: Engine Hood Switch Circuit Low
P257E.plain: The hood switch input reads stuck low — short to ground or stuck-closed switch. The body controller may treat the hood as permanently open and refuse to arm the alarm or close the HV interlock.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P257F.title: Engine Hood Switch Circuit High
P257F.plain: The hood switch input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage or open switch return. The body controller cannot detect when the hood is opened.
causes: Switch wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P2580.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Speed Sensor A Circuit Low
P2580.plain: Turbo speed sensor A signal voltage below the lower limit — short to ground in the signal line or open supply.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2581.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Speed Sensor A Circuit High
P2581.plain: Turbo speed sensor A signal voltage above the upper limit — short to reference voltage or open signal return.
causes: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P2582.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Speed Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P2582.plain: Turbo speed sensor A signal jumps or drops out — vibration, oil mist on the sensor tip, or chafed wiring near the hot turbo.
causes: Oil mist on the sensor tip
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P2583.title: Cruise Control Front Distance Range Sensor Single Sensor or Center
P2583.plain: General fault on the radar/lidar/camera distance-range sensor used by adaptive cruise control. On systems with a single sensor or three sensors with a center unit, this code refers to the central sensor — without it, ACC distance control is disabled and the system falls back to plain cruise.
causes: Dirty sensor surface (radar emblem / camera lens)
Sensor misaligned after a frontal impact

P2584.title: Fuel Additive Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
P2584.plain: The fuel additive control module — typical for diesel cars with a separate Eolys/Cerine additive tank that aids DPF regeneration — has requested the ECM to illuminate the MIL because of an emissions-relevant fault on its side. The original fault is in the additive module itself.
causes: Internal fault in the fuel additive module — read its DTCs

P2585.title: Fuel Additive Control Module Warning Lamp Request
P2585.plain: The fuel additive control module asks for the additive-low warning lamp to be illuminated — the additive tank (Eolys/Cerine, used to lower DPF regen temperature) is approaching empty or has reached a service threshold. Continued driving without refilling will eventually disable DPF regeneration.
causes: Additive tank low — service refill required

P2586.title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Circuit
P2586.plain: General electrical fault on the turbocharger boost control position sensor B — second position sensor on the same actuator (redundant Hall) or on a second turbo (twin-turbo, sequential or two-stage). With B invalid the ECM cannot cross-check actuator A and falls back to limited boost control.
causes: Open or shorted wiring to the position sensor

P2587.title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P2587.plain: Position sensor B is electrically intact, but the reading does not track sensor A or the actuator-command model. Often a misaligned redundant sensor or aged element on a second turbo.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2588.title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Circuit Low
P2588.plain: Position sensor B signal voltage below the lower limit — short to ground or open reference. Boost control tracks commanded vs. actual manifold pressure; persistent deviation means wastegate, vanes, hose or actuator are not delivering the requested pressure.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2589.title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Circuit High
P2589.plain: Position sensor B signal voltage above the upper limit — short to reference voltage or open signal return.
causes: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P258A.title: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit A/Open
P258A.plain: The control circuit driving the electric vacuum pump (used to maintain brake-booster vacuum on direct-injection or hybrid powertrains where the engine is not always running) is open. The ECM cannot run the pump on demand — booster vacuum drops, pedal feel hardens, brake assist may be reduced.
causes: Open control wire to the pump
Failed driver in the control module

P258B.title: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit A Range/Performance
P258B.plain: The vacuum pump control circuit is electrically intact, but the pump response does not match the model — pump runs longer than expected to reach setpoint, current draw rises (mechanically tight) or vacuum does not build at all. Aged motor brushes, dry vanes or a leaking line are typical causes.
causes: Aged motor brushes or dry vanes
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P258C.title: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit A Low
P258C.plain: The electric vacuum pump control circuit reads stuck low — short to ground or low-side driver stuck on. The pump may run continuously, drawing current and overheating, until the ECM disables the channel.

P258D.title: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit A High
P258D.plain: The vacuum pump control circuit reads stuck high — short to battery voltage or open coil/return. The driver cannot pull the line low to start the pump.
causes: Control wire shorted to battery voltage

P258E.title: PTO Enable Switch Performance
P258E.plain: The PTO enable switch is electrically intact but its state does not match operating conditions — for example asserted while the vehicle is rolling above the PTO speed limit, or asserted/de-asserted in fast succession. The ECM rejects the request to avoid unsafe PTO engagement.
causes: Switch operated while vehicle is moving

P258F.title: Torque Management Request Output Signal
P258F.plain: The ECM/PCM produces a torque-management output signal for downstream consumers (TCM during shifts, hybrid module, transfer case) and detects a fault on this output — open, short, or feedback voltage outside expected range. Without it, downstream modules cannot synchronise their behaviour with the engine.
causes: Downstream consumer not loading the line

P2590.title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2590.plain: Position sensor B signal jumps or drops out — vibration on the actuator, oil mist contamination or chafed wiring near the hot turbo.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P2591.title: Cruise Control Front Distance Range Sensor Left
P2591.plain: General fault on the left-side front distance-range sensor used by adaptive cruise. Multi-sensor radar arrays use left/center/right sensors for wider field-of-view and lane discrimination — without left, ACC may degrade to single-target tracking.
causes: Sensor misaligned after a frontal impact

P2592.title: Cruise Control Front Distance Range Sensor Right
P2592.plain: General fault on the right-side front distance-range sensor used by adaptive cruise. Same role as the left sensor but covering the right field-of-view.
causes: Sensor misaligned after a frontal impact

P2593.title: Turbocharger Speed Sensor B Circuit
P2593.plain: General electrical fault on the second turbocharger speed sensor B — used on twin-turbo, sequential or two-stage installations to read the second compressor shaft speed. Same role as sensor A on the second turbo.

P2594.title: Turbocharger Speed Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P2594.plain: Turbo speed sensor B is electrically intact, but the speed reading does not match the boost or air-mass model — same failure mode as sensor A performance fault, applied to the second turbo.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2595.title: Turbocharger Speed Sensor B Circuit Low
P2595.plain: Turbo speed sensor B signal voltage below the lower limit — short to ground or open supply. Boost control tracks commanded vs. actual manifold pressure; persistent deviation means wastegate, vanes, hose or actuator are not delivering the requested pressure.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2596.title: Turbocharger Speed Sensor B Circuit High
P2596.plain: Turbo speed sensor B signal voltage above the upper limit — short to reference voltage or open signal return.
causes: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P2597.title: Turbocharger Speed Sensor B Circuit Intermittent
P2597.plain: Turbo speed sensor B signal jumps or drops out — vibration, oil mist or chafed wiring at the second turbo.
causes: Oil mist on the sensor tip
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P2598.title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Performance - Stuck Low
P2598.plain: Position sensor A reports a value stuck near the low end of its travel even when the actuator is commanded to move. Either the actuator is mechanically stuck closed (wastegate jammed shut, VGT vanes seized at minimum opening) or the sensor itself is pegged low. Boost is uncontrolled — overboost on diesels with VGT, underboost on wastegate-stuck systems.
causes: Actuator mechanically stuck near low end

P2599.title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Performance - Stuck High
P2599.plain: Position sensor A reports a value stuck near the high end of its travel — actuator stuck open (wastegate held wide open, VGT vanes seized at maximum opening) or sensor pegged high. Boost suffers — typically underboost on VGT, overboost-protection-off on wastegate.
causes: Actuator mechanically stuck near high end

P259A.title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Performance - Stuck Low
P259A.plain: Same condition as the A-side stuck-low fault, but on the second sensor / second turbo. Position sensor B reads stuck near the low end while the actuator is commanded.
causes: Actuator mechanically stuck near low end

P259B.title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Performance - Stuck High
P259B.plain: Same as the A-side stuck-high fault, applied to sensor B / turbo B. Boost control tracks commanded vs. actual manifold pressure; persistent deviation means wastegate, vanes, hose or actuator are not delivering the requested pressure.
causes: Actuator mechanically stuck near high end

P259C.title: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Turbocharger A Boost Control
P259C.plain: After start-up the boost-control loop on turbo A takes longer than the calibration limit to transition from open-loop to closed-loop control. Typically a slow-warming actuator (VGT vanes carbonised), a sluggish position sensor or a leaky pneumatic actuator that cannot follow setpoints quickly enough.

P259D.title: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Turbocharger B Boost Control
P259D.plain: Same condition as the turbo A excessive-warm-up fault, applied to the second turbo. Boost control tracks commanded vs. actual manifold pressure; persistent deviation means wastegate, vanes, hose or actuator are not delivering the requested pressure.

P259E.title: Turbocharger A Boost Control Position At Low Limit
P259E.plain: The boost-control actuator on turbo A has been operating at the low end of its travel for too long — the closed-loop controller is saturated against the lower stop trying to reach the boost setpoint. Indicates either a leak (wastegate held closed but boost still escapes) or commanded boost above what the engine can produce.
causes: Boost leak in the charge-air path
Failing turbocharger that cannot produce target boost

P259F.title: Turbocharger A Boost Control Position At High Limit
P259F.plain: The boost-control actuator on turbo A has been operating at the high end of its travel — the controller is saturated against the upper stop trying to bleed off boost. Indicates either a wastegate stuck closed, oversized turbo for the calibration, or commanded boost limits being exceeded by ambient conditions (cold dense air).

P25A0.title: Turbocharger B Boost Control Position At Low Limit
P25A0.plain: Turbocharger B Boost Control Position At Low Limit: the control module has detected this fault condition. This affects turbo/supercharger boost-pressure control.
causes: Boost leak in the charge-air path

P25A1.title: Turbocharger B Boost Control Position At High Limit
P25A1.plain: Turbocharger B Boost Control Position At High Limit: the control module has detected this fault condition. This affects turbo/supercharger boost-pressure control.

P25A2.title: Brake System Control Module A Requested MIL Illumination
P25A2.plain: The primary brake system control module (ABS/ESC/iBooster) has requested the ECM to illuminate the MIL because of an emissions-relevant fault on its side — for example a regenerative braking fault on a hybrid that affects driveline torque flow. The original fault is in the brake module.
causes: Internal fault in the brake module — read its DTCs

P25A3.title: Engine Hood Open
P25A3.plain: After plausibility checks the body controller has concluded that the engine hood is genuinely open while the vehicle is operating. Used to suspend HV operation on hybrids/EVs (HV interlock), block remote engine start, and trigger the alarm if armed.

P25A4.title: Fuel Mode Select Switch Circuit
P25A4.plain: General electrical fault on the fuel mode select switch — used on bi-fuel vehicles (CNG/LPG/H2/gasoline) so the driver can pick the active fuel. With the input invalid, the ECM falls back to the default fuel and disables operator-selectable switching.

P25A5.title: Fuel Mode Select Switch Performance
P25A5.plain: The fuel mode select switch is electrically intact, but its state does not match operating conditions — switched to gas while gas tank is empty, or fast toggling. The ECM rejects the request to avoid stalling.

P25A6.title: Fuel Mode Select Switch Circuit Low
P25A6.plain: Fuel mode switch input reads stuck low — short to ground or stuck-closed contact. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25A7.title: Fuel Mode Select Switch Circuit High
P25A7.plain: Fuel mode switch input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Switch wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P25A8.title: Fuel Mode Select Switch Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P25A8.plain: Fuel mode switch signal jumps or drops out — worn contact or vibration. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P25A9.title: Piston Cooling Oil Control Circuit/Open
P25A9.plain: The piston-cooling oil-jet control circuit is open. Modern engines with under-piston oil jets switch them on under high load to cool the piston crown — controlled by a solenoid valve in the oil gallery. With the circuit broken, jets cannot be commanded on or stay locked off, raising piston temperatures under load.
causes: Open control wire to the solenoid
Pin pushed back out of connector body

P25AA.title: Piston Cooling Oil Control Circuit Low
P25AA.plain: The piston-cooling oil-jet control circuit reads stuck low — short to ground or low-side driver stuck on. The jets may be enabled continuously, raising oil pump load and lowering oil pressure to other consumers.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25AB.title: Piston Cooling Oil Control Circuit High
P25AB.plain: Control circuit stuck high — short to battery voltage or open coil/return. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P25AC.title: Piston Cooling Oil Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P25AC.plain: The control circuit is electrically intact, but the solenoid valve does not open when commanded — confirmed by oil-pressure or oil-temperature feedback that does not change after the activation pulse. Piston cooling does not engage under high load — risk of piston-crown overheating and ring-land cracks.
causes: Solenoid stuck closed by oil sludge
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play

P25AD.title: Piston Cooling Oil Control Circuit Stuck On
P25AD.plain: The piston cooling solenoid does not close when commanded off — jets remain active when not needed. Oil pressure to top-end consumers may sag, and warm-up takes longer because the cooling jets remove heat from the pistons during cold start.
causes: Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play

P25AE.title: Piston Cooling Oil Pressure Too Low
P25AE.plain: With the piston-cooling jets commanded on, the dedicated oil-pressure sensor in that gallery reads below the safe threshold. Insufficient flow to the jets means real piston cooling is not happening — the ECM warns the driver and may reduce torque to protect the pistons.

P25AF.title: Coolant Temperature Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
P25AF.plain: A dedicated coolant-temperature control module (used on engines with electric coolant pumps and electronic thermostats to keep the cylinder head and block at independent setpoints) has requested the ECM to illuminate the MIL because of an emissions-relevant fault on its side. Original fault is in that module.
causes: Internal fault — read the module DTCs

P25B0.title: Fuel Level Sensor A Stuck
P25B0.plain: Fuel level sensor A (typically the float in the main fuel tank section) reports a value that does not change over a long driving distance — the float is mechanically stuck against the tank wall, baffle or pump module. Without level changes the EVAP monitor cannot run and remaining-range estimates are wrong.
causes: Bent float arm catching the tank wall

P25B1.title: Fuel Level Sensor B Stuck
P25B1.plain: Same condition as sensor A stuck, applied to the second fuel level sensor B. Saddle tanks (often AWD vehicles) and large trucks use two sensors — one per tank chamber — averaged for total level. A stuck B leaves only A and reduces accuracy.

P25B2.title: Fuel Level Sensor A or B Stuck
P25B2.plain: The ECM detects that one of the two level sensors is stuck but cannot identify which from the available signals — for example because the saddle-tank algorithm sees implausible delta only intermittently. Both sensors should be inspected.

P25B3.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Wastegate A Stuck Open
P25B3.plain: Wastegate A is mechanically stuck open. Exhaust gas bypasses the turbine even at low load — turbo cannot reach target speed, boost is permanently low and the engine feels asthmatic. Common causes are seized linkage, broken return spring or carbon-locked wastegate flap.
causes: Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement

P25B4.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Wastegate A Stuck Closed
P25B4.plain: Wastegate A is mechanically stuck closed. The turbo cannot bleed off exhaust at high load — boost overshoots the setpoint, risking overboost cut-off and damage to the turbo bearing. Carbon-locked flap, seized linkage or aged actuator are typical causes.
causes: Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement

P25B5.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Wastegate B Stuck Open
P25B5.plain: Same as wastegate A stuck open, applied to the second wastegate (twin-turbo, sequential or two-stage). Boost control tracks commanded vs. actual manifold pressure; persistent deviation means wastegate, vanes, hose or actuator are not delivering the requested pressure.
causes: Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play

P25B6.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Wastegate B Stuck Closed
P25B6.plain: Same as wastegate A stuck closed, applied to the second wastegate. Boost control tracks commanded vs. actual manifold pressure; persistent deviation means wastegate, vanes, hose or actuator are not delivering the requested pressure.
causes: Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play

P25B7.title: Auxiliary Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit
P25B7.plain: General electrical fault on the auxiliary ignition switch On/Start input. Used on commercial vehicles or upfit applications where a second ignition switch (in a sleeper cab, work platform or crew compartment) can crank the engine.

P25B8.title: Auxiliary Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit Low
P25B8.plain: Auxiliary ignition switch On/Start input reads stuck low — short to ground or stuck-closed contact. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25B9.title: Auxiliary Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit High
P25B9.plain: Auxiliary ignition switch On/Start input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P25BA.title: Regeneration Control Switch Circuit/Open
P25BA.plain: The DPF/SCR forced-regeneration request switch — used on commercial vehicles to let the operator force a parked regeneration when the automatic regen has been postponed too often — is open. The ECM cannot honour an operator request for forced regen.
causes: Pin pushed back out of connector body
Cracked solder joint inside the module or sensor

P25BB.title: Regeneration Control Switch Circuit Low
P25BB.plain: Regeneration control switch input reads stuck low — short to ground or stuck-closed contact. The ECM may see a constant regen request which it cannot service while the vehicle is moving.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25BC.title: Regeneration Control Switch Circuit High
P25BC.plain: Regeneration control switch input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Switch wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P25BD.title: Unmetered Fuel - Forced Engine Shutdown
P25BD.plain: The engine controller commanded a forced shutdown after detecting unmetered fuel reaching the combustion chambers. Common on diesels with leaking turbo seals or cracked intercoolers that drip oil into the intake — the engine then runs on the oil and can overspeed.
causes: Turbocharger oil seal leak feeds engine oil into the intake
Oil collected in the intercooler is sucked into the engine on load
Failed PCV / crankcase breather floods intake with oil mist

P25BE.title: Alternative Fuel Disable Control Circuit / Open
P25BE.plain: The controller cannot drive the alternative-fuel disable line that switches a bi-fuel vehicle (CNG, LPG, hydrogen) back to gasoline. An open detected on the control side blocks the safety shutoff for the gas system.
causes: Broken wire or corroded connector on the disable control line
Open coil in the alt-fuel disable relay
Output driver in the alt-fuel control module faulty

P25BF.title: Alternative Fuel Disable Control Circuit High
P25BF.plain: Voltage on the alternative-fuel disable control line is above the expected window. Often a short to battery upstream of the relay or a stuck-on driver in the control module.
causes: Disable control wire shorted to a B+ supply
Output driver stuck on inside the control module
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25C0.title: Alternative Fuel Disable Control Circuit Low
P25C0.plain: Voltage on the alternative-fuel disable control line is below the expected window. Usually a short to ground or a failed driver pulling the line low.
causes: Disable control wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25C1.title: Alternative Fuel Disable Signal Circuit
P25C1.plain: The feedback signal that confirms the alt-fuel disable command was carried out is missing or out of range. The fuel system cannot verify that the gas circuit is shut.
causes: Open feedback wire between relay and control module
Feedback contact in the disable relay corroded or stuck

P25C2.title: Alternative Fuel Disable Signal Circuit High
P25C2.plain: The disable feedback signal sits above its valid window. Typical cause is a short to battery on the feedback wire or a failed pull-up in the input stage.
causes: Feedback wire shorted to a B+ supply
Pull-up resistor in the input stage failed
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25C3.title: Alternative Fuel Disable Signal Circuit Low
P25C3.plain: The disable feedback signal sits below its valid window. Usually a short to ground or an open pull-up that lets the input float low.
causes: Open pull-up resistor in the controller input
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25C4.title: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P25C4.plain: The temperature sensor monitoring the electric brake booster (iBooster, eBooster) returns no usable signal. Without temperature feedback the controller derates booster assist to protect the motor.
causes: Open sensor element or broken sensor wire
Corroded connector on the booster sensor pigtail

P25C5.title: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P25C5.plain: The booster temperature sensor reading is implausible relative to commanded assist or coolant temperature. The signal moves too slowly, sticks, or never reaches expected values during operation.
causes: Sensor drift or contamination on the temperature element
Sensor not seated properly against the booster motor housing
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P25C6.title: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P25C6.plain: The booster temperature signal is below the lower diagnostic threshold. Typical causes are a shorted sensor element or a short to ground in the harness.
causes: Internal short in the sensor element
Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25C7.title: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P25C7.plain: The booster temperature signal is above the upper diagnostic threshold. Common causes are an open sensor or a short to a 5 V reference in the harness.
causes: Sensor signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25C8.title: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P25C8.plain: The booster temperature signal jumps or drops out for short moments. Usually a loose connector or a chafed wire that opens during vibration or thermal expansion.
causes: Sensor connector not fully seated or pin tension lost
Harness chafed against booster housing or pedal bracket
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P25C9.title: Brake System Control Module B Requested MIL Illumination
P25C9.plain: A second brake system control module (typically the redundant secondary unit on by-wire or AV-grade brake systems) has signalled an emissions-relevant fault and requested the engine controller to switch on the MIL.
causes: Active DTC stored in the secondary brake module
Communication loss interpreted as MIL request

P25CA.title: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit / Open Bank 1
P25CA.plain: The controller cannot drive the park-lock pin that secures the intake camshaft phaser on bank 1 in its base position at engine off. Without the lock, the next start can suffer poor combustion or rough idle until the phaser builds oil pressure.
causes: Open coil in the park-lock solenoid
Broken control wire between ECU and solenoid

P25CB.title: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit Low Bank 1
P25CB.plain: The intake camshaft park-lock control line on bank 1 is below the expected voltage window. Usually a short to ground or a low-side driver shorted internally.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25CC.title: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit High Bank 1
P25CC.plain: The intake camshaft park-lock control line on bank 1 is above the expected voltage window. Typical causes are a short to battery or a stuck-on driver in the controller.
causes: Control wire shorted to a B+ supply
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25CD.title: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit / Open Bank 2
P25CD.plain: The controller cannot drive the park-lock pin that secures the intake camshaft phaser on bank 2 in its base position at engine off. Without the lock, the next start can suffer poor combustion or rough idle until the phaser builds oil pressure.
causes: Open coil in the park-lock solenoid
Broken control wire between ECU and solenoid

P25CE.title: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit Low Bank 2
P25CE.plain: The intake camshaft park-lock control line on bank 2 is below the expected voltage window. Usually a short to ground or a low-side driver shorted internally.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25CF.title: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit High Bank 2
P25CF.plain: The intake camshaft park-lock control line on bank 2 is above the expected voltage window. Typical causes are a short to battery or a stuck-on driver in the controller.
causes: Control wire shorted to a B+ supply
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25D0.title: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit / Open Bank 1
P25D0.plain: The controller cannot drive the park-lock pin that secures the exhaust camshaft phaser on bank 1 in its base position at engine off. Without the lock, the next start can suffer poor combustion or rough idle until the phaser builds oil pressure.
causes: Open coil in the park-lock solenoid
Broken control wire between ECU and solenoid

P25D1.title: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit Low Bank 1
P25D1.plain: The exhaust camshaft park-lock control line on bank 1 is below the expected voltage window. Usually a short to ground or a low-side driver shorted internally.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25D2.title: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit High Bank 1
P25D2.plain: The exhaust camshaft park-lock control line on bank 1 is above the expected voltage window. Typical causes are a short to battery or a stuck-on driver in the controller.
causes: Control wire shorted to a B+ supply
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25D3.title: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit / Open Bank 2
P25D3.plain: The controller cannot drive the park-lock pin that secures the exhaust camshaft phaser on bank 2 in its base position at engine off. Without the lock, the next start can suffer poor combustion or rough idle until the phaser builds oil pressure.
causes: Open coil in the park-lock solenoid
Broken control wire between ECU and solenoid

P25D4.title: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit Low Bank 2
P25D4.plain: The exhaust camshaft park-lock control line on bank 2 is below the expected voltage window. Usually a short to ground or a low-side driver shorted internally.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25D5.title: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit High Bank 2
P25D5.plain: The exhaust camshaft park-lock control line on bank 2 is above the expected voltage window. Typical causes are a short to battery or a stuck-on driver in the controller.
causes: Control wire shorted to a B+ supply
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25D6.title: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Stop Performance
P25D6.plain: During self-calibration of the exhaust heat exchanger bypass valve A, the position sensor never reached the expected mechanical stop. The controller cannot zero the position reference, so commanded openings will be inaccurate.
causes: Soot or carbon deposits prevent valve from reaching the stop
Worn linkage between actuator and valve flap
Position sensor not aligned with valve shaft

P25D7.title: Fuel Level Sensor C Circuit
P25D7.plain: A third fuel level sensor (C) used on multi-tank trucks, dual-saddle SUVs, or auxiliary fuel systems returns no usable signal. Without it, calculated fuel level and EVAP monitor enabling will be off.
causes: Open sender resistor or broken float

P25D8.title: Fuel Level Sensor C Performance
P25D8.plain: The third fuel level sensor reading does not change as expected with consumption or refuelling. Float may be sticking, or the resistor track has localised wear.
causes: Float arm stuck on baffle or fuel pump module
Worn spot on the resistor track at common fill level

P25D9.title: Fuel Level Sensor C Circuit Low
P25D9.plain: The third fuel level sensor signal is below the lower diagnostic threshold. Usually a shorted sender or a short to ground in the harness.
causes: Internal short in the sender resistor
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25DA.title: Fuel Level Sensor C Circuit High
P25DA.plain: The third fuel level sensor signal is above the upper diagnostic threshold. Common causes are an open sender or a short to the 5 V reference.
causes: Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25DB.title: Fuel Level Sensor C Circuit Intermittent
P25DB.plain: The third fuel level sensor signal jumps or drops out for short moments. Usually a loose connector or a chafed wire that opens during driving vibration.
causes: Tank module connector not fully seated
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P25DC.title: Fuel Level Sensor C Stuck
P25DC.plain: The third fuel level sensor reads a constant value across known consumption or refuelling events. Float arm or resistor wiper is mechanically stuck.
causes: Float arm jammed against tank wall, baffle or pump module
Resistor wiper seized by varnish from old fuel

P25DD.title: A Camshaft Position - Stuck In Locked Position Bank 1
P25DD.plain: Camshaft phaser A on bank 1 will not unlock from its base position. The phaser stays at the park-lock angle and cannot be advanced or retarded as commanded.
causes: Park-lock pin stuck in the locked groove
Low oil pressure cannot push the lock pin out
Oil control valve blocked by debris

P25DE.title: A Camshaft Position - Unable to Achieve Locked Position Bank 1
P25DE.plain: Camshaft phaser A on bank 1 cannot reach its base position at engine shutdown so the lock pin never engages. Next cold start may run rough until oil pressure builds.
causes: Worn vanes or housing inside the phaser
Sludge or contaminated oil prevents return to base

P25DF.title: A Camshaft Position Control Performance Bank 1
P25DF.plain: Camshaft phaser A on bank 1 follows the commanded angle too slowly, oscillates, or shows steady-state error outside tolerance. Closed-loop control of cam timing is degraded.
causes: Oil control valve spool sticks under varnish
Stretched timing chain shifts cam reference
Wrong oil viscosity slows phaser response

P25E0.title: A Camshaft Position - Stuck In Locked Position Bank 2
P25E0.plain: Camshaft phaser A on bank 2 will not unlock from its base position. The phaser stays at the park-lock angle and cannot be advanced or retarded as commanded.
causes: Park-lock pin stuck in the locked groove
Low oil pressure cannot push the lock pin out
Oil control valve blocked by debris

P25E1.title: A Camshaft Position - Unable to Achieve Locked Position Bank 2
P25E1.plain: Camshaft phaser A on bank 2 cannot reach its base position at engine shutdown so the lock pin never engages. Next cold start may run rough until oil pressure builds.
causes: Worn vanes or housing inside the phaser
Sludge or contaminated oil prevents return to base

P25E2.title: A Camshaft Position Control Performance Bank 2
P25E2.plain: Camshaft phaser A on bank 2 follows the commanded angle too slowly, oscillates, or shows steady-state error outside tolerance. Closed-loop control of cam timing is degraded.
causes: Oil control valve spool sticks under varnish
Stretched timing chain shifts cam reference
Wrong oil viscosity slows phaser response

P25E3.title: B Camshaft Position - Stuck In Locked Position Bank 1
P25E3.plain: Camshaft phaser B on bank 1 will not unlock from its base position. The phaser stays at the park-lock angle and cannot be advanced or retarded as commanded.
causes: Park-lock pin stuck in the locked groove
Low oil pressure cannot push the lock pin out
Oil control valve blocked by debris

P25E4.title: B Camshaft Position - Unable to Achieve Locked Position Bank 1
P25E4.plain: Camshaft phaser B on bank 1 cannot reach its base position at engine shutdown so the lock pin never engages. Next cold start may run rough until oil pressure builds.
causes: Worn vanes or housing inside the phaser
Sludge or contaminated oil prevents return to base

P25E5.title: B Camshaft Position Control Performance Bank 1
P25E5.plain: Camshaft phaser B on bank 1 follows the commanded angle too slowly, oscillates, or shows steady-state error outside tolerance. Closed-loop control of cam timing is degraded.
causes: Oil control valve spool sticks under varnish
Stretched timing chain shifts cam reference
Wrong oil viscosity slows phaser response

P25E6.title: B Camshaft Position - Stuck In Locked Position Bank 2
P25E6.plain: Camshaft phaser B on bank 2 will not unlock from its base position. The phaser stays at the park-lock angle and cannot be advanced or retarded as commanded.
causes: Park-lock pin stuck in the locked groove
Low oil pressure cannot push the lock pin out
Oil control valve blocked by debris

P25E7.title: B Camshaft Position - Unable to Achieve Locked Position Bank 2
P25E7.plain: Camshaft phaser B on bank 2 cannot reach its base position at engine shutdown so the lock pin never engages. Next cold start may run rough until oil pressure builds.
causes: Worn vanes or housing inside the phaser
Sludge or contaminated oil prevents return to base

P25E8.title: B Camshaft Position Control Performance Bank 2
P25E8.plain: Camshaft phaser B on bank 2 follows the commanded angle too slowly, oscillates, or shows steady-state error outside tolerance. Closed-loop control of cam timing is degraded.
causes: Oil control valve spool sticks under varnish
Stretched timing chain shifts cam reference
Wrong oil viscosity slows phaser response

P25E9.title: Supercharger Disconnect Clutch Stuck Open
P25E9.plain: The clutch that engages the mechanical supercharger to the engine drive will not close. The supercharger stays disengaged so boost from this stage is unavailable, which limits torque and may also affect cooling pump drives shared with the same belt.
causes: Worn friction surfaces leave the air gap too large to attract

P25EA.title: Supercharger Disconnect Clutch Stuck Closed
P25EA.plain: The clutch that engages the mechanical supercharger to the engine drive will not open. The supercharger remains coupled at all loads, increasing parasitic loss and fuel consumption when boost is not needed.
causes: Armature plate seized to the pulley face
Driver stuck on keeps clutch energised
Failed pulley bearing welds clutch surfaces

P25EB.title: Supercharger Disconnect Clutch Circuit Range/Performance
P25EB.plain: The supercharger clutch control current does not match the commanded value within tolerance. Either coil resistance has drifted or the driver feedback is implausible.
causes: Coil resistance increased due to thermal damage
High-resistance contact in the clutch connector
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P25EC.title: Supercharger Disconnect Clutch Circuit Low
P25EC.plain: Voltage on the supercharger clutch control line is below the expected window. Usually a short to ground or a shorted clutch coil.
causes: Internal short in the clutch coil
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25ED.title: Supercharger Disconnect Clutch Circuit High
P25ED.plain: Voltage on the supercharger clutch control line is above the expected window. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open coil that lets the driver float high.
causes: Control wire shorted to a B+ supply
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25EE.title: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit B / Open
P25EE.plain: The controller cannot drive the secondary electric vacuum pump (B). Brake servo or HVAC actuators that depend on engine vacuum may not get enough vacuum during low-load operation or with engine off in stop-start mode.
causes: Open pump motor winding or worn brushes
Broken control wire between ECU and pump

P25EF.title: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit B Range/Performance
P25EF.plain: The secondary vacuum pump does not produce the expected vacuum within the commanded run time. Leak in the pump line or worn pump diaphragm reduces output.
causes: Worn diaphragm or vanes inside the pump
Cracked vacuum hose or loose connection
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P25F0.title: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit B Low
P25F0.plain: Voltage on the secondary vacuum pump control line is below the expected window. Usually a short to ground or a shorted motor winding.
causes: Internal short in pump motor winding

P25F1.title: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit B High
P25F1.plain: Voltage on the secondary vacuum pump control line is above the expected window. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open motor that lets the driver float high.
causes: Control wire shorted to a B+ supply
Open motor winding or worn brushes

P25F2.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor C Circuit
P25F2.plain: A third boost pressure sensor (C) used on twin-stage or sequential boost systems returns no usable signal. Without it, boost control of the third stage runs open-loop or is disabled.
causes: Open sensor element or broken signal wire

P25F3.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P25F3.plain: The third boost pressure sensor reading is implausible compared with manifold pressure or commanded boost. Either drift, leak in the sensing line, or contamination on the sensor diaphragm.
causes: Sensing hose blocked by oil residue
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P25F4.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor C Circuit Low
P25F4.plain: The third boost pressure sensor signal is below the lower diagnostic threshold. Usually a shorted sensor element or a short to ground.
causes: Internal short in the sensor element
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25F5.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor C Circuit High
P25F5.plain: The third boost pressure sensor signal is above the upper diagnostic threshold. Common causes are an open sensor or a short to the 5 V reference.
causes: Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25F6.title: AIR System B
P25F6.plain: A general fault in the second secondary air injection (AIR) circuit. Detected by the O2 sensors which expect a lean swing during cold-start AIR pump operation but do not see one.
causes: Failed AIR pump motor or impeller
Check valve seized by exhaust soot
Corroded or cracked air injection pipe

P25F7.title: AIR System B Incorrect Flow Detected
P25F7.plain: The second AIR system delivers measurably more or less air than expected. Often a partially blocked pipe, a worn pump, or a leak between pump and check valve.
causes: Air pipe partially blocked by carbon
Leak between pump and check valve

P25F8.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve C Control Circuit
P25F8.plain: A third bypass (recirculation or wastegate) valve used in three-stage charging systems is not responding to control commands. Boost balancing across stages can no longer be achieved.
causes: Open or shorted wiring to the valve

P25F9.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve C Control Circuit Low
P25F9.plain: Voltage on the third bypass valve control line is below the expected window. Usually a short to ground or a shorted solenoid coil.
causes: Internal short in the solenoid coil
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25FA.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve C Control Circuit High
P25FA.plain: Voltage on the third bypass valve control line is above the expected window. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open solenoid coil.
causes: Control wire shorted to a B+ supply
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P25FB.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve C Control Circuit Range/Performance
P25FB.plain: The third bypass valve current does not match the commanded value within tolerance. Drifted coil resistance or high-resistance contact in the connector.
causes: Coil resistance changed by thermal stress
High-resistance contact in the valve connector
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P25FC.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve C - Mechanical
P25FC.plain: The third bypass valve is mechanically jammed. Solenoid is energised correctly but the valve flap or disc does not move as expected.
causes: Carbon buildup blocks the valve flap

P25FD.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve C Temperature Too High
P25FD.plain: The third bypass valve has reached over-temperature. Either coil duty cycle is too high for too long, or cooling air flow around the valve is restricted.
causes: Sustained high duty cycle from charge balancing strategy
Cooling air channel blocked by debris

P25FE.title: Supercharger Disconnect Clutch
P25FE.plain: A general performance fault in the supercharger disconnect clutch. Engagement or release is slow, sticky, or out of tolerance without a clear electrical-side cause.
causes: Worn friction surfaces or air gap drift
Oil or debris on the clutch face

P25FF.title: Electrical System Voltage Stabilizer Control Module Performance
P25FF.plain: The voltage stabiliser module (DC/DC converter for stop-start engine cranking events) does not maintain the regulated 12 V output during high transient loads. Sensitive electronics may reset during cranking.
causes: Battery condition causes input voltage to drop too far
Internal fault in the converter switching stage

P2600.title: Coolant Pump A Control Circuit / Open
P2600.plain: The controller cannot drive the electric coolant pump A control line. Without circulation, engine and aftertreatment can overheat or warm up incorrectly.
causes: Broken control wire to the pump

P2601.title: Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P2601.plain: The electric coolant pump A is commanded on but does not run. Coolant temperature climbs faster than expected with no flow detected.
causes: Pump motor seized by debris or sediment
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement

P2602.title: Coolant Pump Control Circuit Open
P2602.plain: The ECU detects an open circuit on the electric coolant pump control line. Without pump control the engine cannot actively manage warm-up and cool-down phases.
causes: Pin pushed back out of connector body

P2603.title: Coolant Pump Control Circuit Low
P2603.plain: The electric coolant pump drive line reads below the lower threshold — typically a short to ground or a failed driver stage.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2604.title: Coolant Pump Control Circuit High
P2604.plain: The electric coolant pump drive line reads above the upper threshold — usually a short to positive or a stuck-on driver stage.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2605.title: Intake Air Heater B Circuit / Open
P2605.plain: The controller cannot drive the secondary intake air heater (heater grid B) used on diesel engines for cold-start support. The grid stays cold so cold-start emissions and white smoke increase.
causes: Failed heater relay or open coil

P2606.title: Intake Air Heater B Circuit Range/Performance
P2606.plain: The secondary intake air heater current does not match expected resistance. Either the grid is partially open or the relay contacts have high resistance.
causes: Partial element failure raises grid resistance
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2607.title: Intake Air Heater B Circuit Low
P2607.plain: Voltage on the secondary intake air heater control line is below the expected window. Usually a short to ground or a shorted relay coil.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2608.title: Intake Air Heater B Circuit High
P2608.plain: Voltage on the secondary intake air heater control line is above the expected window. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open relay coil.
causes: Control wire shorted to a B+ supply
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2609.title: Intake Air Heater System Performance
P2609.plain: The intake air heater system did not raise intake temperature by the expected amount during cold-start support. Suggests low current draw, poor connection to the grid, or a failed temperature feedback path.
causes: High-resistance battery feed to the heater
Intake air temperature sensor reads with offset

P260A.title: PTO Control Circuit / Open
P260A.plain: The controller cannot drive the power take-off (PTO) engagement line on commercial vehicles. The PTO will not engage even when commanded by the body controller or operator switch.
causes: Open coil in the PTO engagement solenoid
Broken wire to the PTO solenoid

P260B.title: PTO Control Circuit Low
P260B.plain: Voltage on the PTO engagement control line is below the expected window. Usually a short to ground or a shorted solenoid coil.
causes: Internal short in the solenoid coil
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P260C.title: PTO Control Circuit High
P260C.plain: Voltage on the PTO engagement control line is above the expected window. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open solenoid coil.
causes: Control wire shorted to a B+ supply
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P260D.title: PTO Engaged Lamp Control Circuit
P260D.plain: The dashboard PTO engaged lamp control circuit is faulty. Driver may not see whether the PTO is currently driving an external accessory.
causes: Open or shorted wire between cluster and ECU

P260E.title: Particulate Filter Regeneration Lamp Control Circuit
P260E.plain: The DPF regeneration warning lamp circuit is faulty. The driver may not be alerted to a required highway run that supports passive regeneration.
causes: Open or shorted wire to the cluster

P260F.title: EVAP System Monitoring Processor Performance
P260F.plain: The dedicated EVAP monitoring processor (often a small auxiliary CPU inside the engine controller or a separate module) does not pass its self-test or runs out of step with the main monitor logic.
causes: Internal fault in the monitoring processor
Module software outdated, reflash may resolve

P2610.title: ECM/PCM Internal Engine Off Timer Performance
P2610.plain: The engine controller's internal soak-time/engine-off timer fails its plausibility check — for example readings claim instant cool-down or never-cooled. Cold-start enrichment, EVAP and catalyst monitors depend on this timer; a fault freezes those readiness monitors.

P2611.title: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve A Control Circuit / Open
P2611.plain: The A/C refrigerant distribution valve A (used to switch refrigerant flow between front and rear evaporators or between cabin and battery cooling on EVs) cannot be driven by the controller.
causes: Open coil in the valve solenoid

P2612.title: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve A Control Circuit Low
P2612.plain: Voltage on the A/C distribution valve A control line is below the expected window. Usually a short to ground or a shorted solenoid coil.
causes: Internal short in the valve solenoid
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2613.title: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve A Control Circuit High
P2613.plain: Voltage on the A/C distribution valve A control line is above the expected window. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open solenoid coil.
causes: Control wire shorted to a B+ supply
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2614.title: Camshaft Position Output Circuit/Open
P2614.plain: The camshaft position output signal sent from the ECU to other modules is interrupted. Other systems that rely on the cam reference (e.g. transmission, hybrid module) do not receive a valid signal.
causes: Pin pushed back out of connector body

P2615.title: Camshaft A Position Signal Output Circuit Low Bank 1
P2615.plain: The buffered camshaft A position output that the engine controller sends to other modules (transmission, body, ignition module) is below the expected level on bank 1. Other modules cannot use the cam phase reference for synchronisation.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2616.title: Camshaft A Position Signal Output Circuit High Bank 1
P2616.plain: The buffered camshaft A position output is above the expected level on bank 1. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open output stage.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2617.title: Crankshaft Position Signal Output Circuit / Open
P2617.plain: The buffered crankshaft position output that the engine controller sends to ignition modules and the transmission cannot drive its line. Open detected on the output side.
causes: Open wire between ECU and downstream module

P2618.title: Crankshaft Position Signal Output Circuit Low
P2618.plain: The buffered crankshaft position output is below the expected level. Usually a short to ground on the output line or a failed buffer.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2619.title: Crankshaft Position Signal Output Circuit High
P2619.plain: The buffered crankshaft position output is above the expected level. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open output stage.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P261A.title: Coolant Pump B Control Circuit / Open
P261A.plain: The controller cannot drive the second electric coolant pump (B). Often used for aftertreatment, turbo cool-down, or hybrid battery loops — fault stops circulation in that loop.
causes: Broken control wire to the pump

P261B.title: Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P261B.plain: The second electric coolant pump is commanded on but does not run. Cooling demand of the connected loop is not satisfied.
causes: Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement

P261C.title: Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Low
P261C.plain: Voltage on the second coolant pump control line is below the expected window. Usually a short to ground or a shorted motor winding.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P261D.title: Coolant Pump B Control Circuit High
P261D.plain: Voltage on the second coolant pump control line is above the expected window. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open motor winding.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P261E.title: Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Stuck On
P261E.plain: The second coolant pump runs even when no command is active. Driver is stuck on or the wire is shorted to a permanent supply.
causes: Control wire shorted to a permanent B+ supply
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement

P261F.title: Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Stuck On
P261F.plain: The first coolant pump runs even when no command is active. Driver is stuck on or the wire is shorted to a permanent supply.
causes: Control wire shorted to a permanent B+ supply
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement

P2620.title: Throttle Position Output Circuit
P2620.plain: A general electrical fault on the ECU output that broadcasts the throttle position signal to other modules — for example to the transmission control or hybrid drive controller.

P2621.title: Throttle Position Output Circuit Low
P2621.plain: The buffered throttle position output that the engine controller sends to the transmission and body modules is below the expected level. Usually a short to ground or a failed output stage.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2622.title: Throttle Position Output Circuit High
P2622.plain: The buffered throttle position output is above the expected level. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open output stage.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2623.title: Injector Control Pressure Regulator Circuit / Open
P2623.plain: The Injector Control Pressure (ICP) regulator on hydraulically actuated injectors (HEUI diesel) or the high-pressure regulator on common-rail systems cannot be driven. Injection pressure cannot be controlled, engine may not start.
causes: Open coil in the pressure regulator

P2624.title: Injector Control Pressure Regulator Circuit Low
P2624.plain: Voltage on the ICP regulator control line is below the expected window. Usually a short to ground or a shorted regulator coil.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2625.title: Injector Control Pressure Regulator Circuit High
P2625.plain: Voltage on the ICP regulator control line is above the expected window. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open regulator coil.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2626.title: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit/Open Bank 1 Sensor 1
P2626.plain: The ECU detects an open in the pumping current trim circuit of the wide-band oxygen sensor on bank 1 sensor 1. Without trim correction, the lambda value reported by the sensor is not accurate.
causes: Pin pushed back out of connector body

P2627.title: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Low Bank 1 Sensor 1
P2627.plain: On a wide-band (broadband) O2 sensor, the trim resistor circuit that calibrates the pumping current is reading low on bank 1 sensor 1. Air-fuel feedback gain is wrong, causing rich or lean offsets.
causes: Short in the calibration trim resistor
Water intrusion in the sensor connector
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2628.title: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit High Bank 1 Sensor 1
P2628.plain: The wide-band trim resistor circuit on bank 1 sensor 1 reads high. Air-fuel feedback gain is wrong, causing offsets that the controller cannot compensate.
causes: Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P2629.title: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit / Open Bank 2 Sensor 1
P2629.plain: The wide-band trim resistor circuit on bank 2 sensor 1 is open. Air-fuel feedback for bank 2 cannot be calibrated, fuel control runs degraded.

P262A.title: Fuel Injector - Pilot Injection Not Learned
P262A.plain: The pilot (pre) injection learning routine on a common-rail diesel did not complete successfully. Without learned pilot quantity, combustion noise increases and NOx may rise.
causes: Injector flow drift outside learning window
Unstable rail pressure during learning cycle

P262B.title: Control Module Power Off Timer Performance
P262B.plain: The internal power-down timer of the engine controller does not run as expected. The module either stays awake too long after key-off (battery drain) or shuts down too early (no aftertreatment cool-down or learn-write).

P262C.title: Sensor Reference Voltage G Circuit / Open
P262C.plain: The 5 V reference G output that the engine controller supplies to a group of sensors is open. All sensors fed from this rail will report invalid readings.
causes: Open wire on the reference rail
Open inside the ECU reference output

P262D.title: Sensor Reference Voltage G Circuit Low
P262D.plain: The 5 V reference G voltage is below the expected level. Usually a short to ground or excessive load from a downstream sensor pulling the rail down.
causes: Sensor on the rail shorted internally to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P262E.title: Sensor Reference Voltage G Circuit High
P262E.plain: The 5 V reference G voltage is above the expected level. Typical causes are a short to battery or an internal regulator failure.
causes: Reference wire shorted to a B+ supply
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P262F.title: Sensor Reference Voltage G Circuit Range/Performance
P262F.plain: The 5 V reference G voltage is within range but unstable or offset against expected. Loose ground or marginal regulator load.
causes: High-resistance ground for the reference rail
One sensor draws excessive current and shifts the rail
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2630.title: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Low Bank 2 Sensor 1
P2630.plain: The wide-band trim resistor circuit on bank 2 sensor 1 reads low. Air-fuel feedback gain on bank 2 is wrong, causing rich or lean offsets.
causes: Short in the calibration trim resistor
Water intrusion in the sensor connector
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2631.title: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit High Bank 2 Sensor 1
P2631.plain: The wide-band trim resistor circuit on bank 2 sensor 1 reads high. Air-fuel feedback gain on bank 2 is wrong, the controller cannot compensate the offset.
causes: Supply wire pinched against B+ source

P2632.title: Fuel Pump B Control Circuit / Open
P2632.plain: The controller cannot drive the secondary fuel pump (B). Common on dual-tank trucks, GDI lift-pump systems, or alt-fuel installations — fault stops fuel delivery from this stage.

P2633.title: Fuel Pump B Control Circuit Low
P2633.plain: Voltage on the second fuel pump control line is below the expected window. Usually a short to ground or a shorted motor winding.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2634.title: Fuel Pump B Control Circuit High
P2634.plain: Voltage on the second fuel pump control line is above the expected window. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open motor winding.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2635.title: Fuel Pump A Low Flow / Performance
P2635.plain: The ECU detects insufficient fuel flow from fuel pump A. Either the pump is worn out, the supply line is restricted, or the pressure regulator does not allow proper flow.

P2636.title: Fuel Pump B Low Flow/Performance
P2636.plain: The second fuel pump runs but does not deliver expected volume or pressure. Worn pump, restricted filter, or leaking pressure regulator.
causes: Restricted in-tank or in-line fuel filter
Pressure regulator leaks back to tank

P2637.title: Torque Management Feedback Signal A
P2637.plain: The torque feedback signal A from the transmission or other torque user is missing or invalid. The engine controller cannot reduce torque on shift requests, which can cause harsh shifts.
causes: Required CAN message not received in time
Source module reports an internal fault

P2638.title: Torque Management Feedback Signal A Range/Performance
P2638.plain: The torque feedback signal A is present but its value is implausible against measured engine load and speed. Sender calibration or sensor offset is suspected.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2639.title: Torque Management Feedback Signal A Low
P2639.plain: The torque feedback signal A reads below its valid range. Either the source reports a value below physical possibility or the bus signal is stuck low.
causes: Source module sends invalid low value
Signal stuck low on the bus

P263A.title: MIL Control Circuit Low
P263A.plain: Voltage on the malfunction indicator lamp control line is below the expected window. Usually a short to ground or a shorted bulb driver.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P263B.title: MIL Control Circuit High
P263B.plain: Voltage on the malfunction indicator lamp control line is above the expected window. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open lamp.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P263C.title: Glow Plug Control Driver Performance
P263C.plain: The glow plug control driver does not respond to commands within tolerance. Cold-start glow function is degraded so cold starting can be delayed and white smoke increases.
causes: Aged driver shows degraded switching behaviour

P263D.title: Reductant Heater Driver Performance
P263D.plain: The reductant (AdBlue) tank or line heater driver does not switch as expected. AdBlue may freeze in cold weather, blocking SCR dosing.
causes: Aged driver shows degraded switching behaviour
Heater element resistance drifted out of range

P263E.title: Glow Plug Control Module 1 Over Temperature
P263E.plain: The first glow plug control module reports over-temperature. Sustained current draw or insufficient cooling has driven the module above its rated temperature.
causes: One glow plug shorted to ground forces module overcurrent
Cooling air channel blocked by debris

P263F.title: Glow Plug Control Module 2 Over Temperature
P263F.plain: The second glow plug control module reports over-temperature. Sustained current draw or insufficient cooling has driven the module above its rated temperature.
causes: One glow plug shorted to ground forces module overcurrent
Cooling air channel blocked by debris

P2640.title: Torque Management Feedback Signal A High
P2640.plain: The torque feedback signal A reads above its valid range. Source module sends an implausibly high value or the bus signal is stuck high.
causes: Source module sends invalid high value
Signal stuck high on the bus

P2641.title: Torque Management Feedback Signal B
P2641.plain: The torque feedback signal B from a second torque user is missing or invalid. The engine controller cannot coordinate torque reduction with this user.
causes: Required CAN message not received in time
Source module reports an internal fault

P2642.title: Torque Management Feedback Signal B Range/Performance
P2642.plain: The torque feedback signal B is present but its value is implausible against measured engine load and speed. Sender calibration or sensor offset is suspected.
causes: Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2643.title: Torque Management Feedback Signal B Low
P2643.plain: The torque feedback signal B reads below its valid range. Source sends a value below physical possibility or the bus signal is stuck low.
causes: Source module sends invalid low value
Signal stuck low on the bus

P2644.title: Torque Management Feedback Signal B High
P2644.plain: The torque feedback signal B reads above its valid range. Source sends an implausibly high value or the bus signal is stuck high.
causes: Source module sends invalid high value
Signal stuck high on the bus

P2645.title: A Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit / Open Bank 1
P2645.plain: The controller cannot drive the rocker arm switching actuator A on bank 1 (used in cylinder deactivation systems such as VTEC, AFM, MDS). The valve lift mode cannot be switched.
causes: Open coil in oil control valve

P2646.title: A Rocker Arm Actuator System Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1
P2646.plain: The rocker arm actuator A on bank 1 is commanded to engage (high lift or all-cylinder mode) but does not switch. Engine stays in low-lift or deactivated mode under load, causing reduced power.
causes: Low oil pressure cannot move the actuator
Mechanical lock pin stuck in unactivated position
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement

P2647.title: A Rocker Arm Actuator System Stuck On Bank 1
P2647.plain: On variable valve lift systems (e.g. Honda VTEC) the ECU detects that the bank 1 rocker arm actuator is stuck in the engaged (high lift) position. Idle quality and fuel economy are affected.
causes: Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement

P2648.title: A Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit Low Bank 1
P2648.plain: Voltage on the rocker arm actuator A control line on bank 1 is below the expected window. Usually a short to ground or a shorted solenoid coil.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2649.title: A Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit High Bank 1
P2649.plain: Voltage on the rocker arm actuator A control line on bank 1 is above the expected window. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open solenoid coil.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P264A.title: A Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Bank 1
P264A.plain: The position sensor that confirms the A rocker arm switching state on bank 1 returns no usable signal. Closed-loop control of valve lift cannot verify the state.

P264B.title: A Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1
P264B.plain: The position sensor reading does not transition cleanly between the two valve lift modes on bank 1. Sensor drift or mechanical wear leaves the signal between expected values.
causes: Sensor signal drift after thermal aging
Worn lock pin reduces travel between modes
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P264C.title: A Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Low Bank 1
P264C.plain: The position sensor signal is below the lower diagnostic threshold. Usually a shorted sensor or short to ground in the harness.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P264D.title: A Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit High Bank 1
P264D.plain: The position sensor signal is above the upper diagnostic threshold. Common causes are an open sensor or a short to the 5 V reference.
causes: Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P264E.title: A Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic Bank 1
P264E.plain: The position sensor signal jumps or drops out intermittently. Usually a loose connector or a chafed wire in the harness.
causes: Harness chafed against valve cover or cam carrier
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P264F.title: Engine Serial Number Not Programmed or Incompatible
P264F.plain: The engine controller cannot read a valid engine serial number from its non-volatile memory, or the stored value does not match the expected pattern. Calibration sets keyed to the serial number cannot be applied.
causes: Replacement ECU not programmed at install

P2650.title: B Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit / Open Bank 1
P2650.plain: The controller cannot drive the rocker arm switching actuator B on bank 1. The second valve lift mode cannot be commanded.
causes: Open coil in oil control valve

P2651.title: B Rocker Arm Actuator System Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1
P2651.plain: The rocker arm actuator B on bank 1 is commanded to engage but does not switch. Engine stays in the wrong lift or cylinder mode under load.
causes: Low oil pressure cannot move the actuator
Mechanical lock pin stuck in unactivated position
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement

P2652.title: B Rocker Arm Actuator System Stuck On Bank 1
P2652.plain: The rocker arm actuator B on bank 1 stays in the activated state when commanded off. Engine cannot return to the alternate lift or cylinder mode.
causes: Mechanical lock pin stuck in activated position
Oil control valve spool stuck open
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement

P2653.title: B Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit Low Bank 1
P2653.plain: Voltage on the rocker arm actuator B control line on bank 1 is below the expected window. Usually a short to ground or a shorted solenoid coil.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2654.title: B Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit High Bank 1
P2654.plain: Voltage on the rocker arm actuator B control line on bank 1 is above the expected window. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open solenoid coil.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2655.title: A Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit / Open Bank 2
P2655.plain: The controller cannot drive the rocker arm switching actuator A on bank 2. The valve lift mode cannot be switched on this bank.
causes: Open coil in oil control valve

P2656.title: A Rocker Arm Actuator System Performance/Stuck Off Bank 2
P2656.plain: The rocker arm actuator A on bank 2 is commanded to engage but does not switch. Engine stays in the wrong lift mode under load on this bank.
causes: Low oil pressure cannot move the actuator
Mechanical lock pin stuck in unactivated position
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement

P2657.title: A Rocker Arm Actuator System Stuck On Bank 2
P2657.plain: The rocker arm actuator A on bank 2 stays in the activated state when commanded off.
causes: Mechanical lock pin stuck in activated position
Oil control valve spool stuck open
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement

P2658.title: A Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit Low Bank 2
P2658.plain: Voltage on the rocker arm actuator A control line on bank 2 is below the expected window. Usually a short to ground or a shorted solenoid coil.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2659.title: A Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit High Bank 2
P2659.plain: Voltage on the rocker arm actuator A control line on bank 2 is above the expected window. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open solenoid coil.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P265A.title: B Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Bank 1
P265A.plain: The position sensor that confirms the B rocker arm switching state on bank 1 returns no usable signal.

P265B.title: B Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1
P265B.plain: The position sensor reading does not transition cleanly between the two valve lift modes for actuator B on bank 1.
causes: Sensor signal drift after thermal aging
Worn lock pin reduces travel between modes
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P265C.title: B Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Low Bank 1
P265C.plain: The position sensor signal for actuator B on bank 1 is below the lower diagnostic threshold. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P265D.title: B Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit High Bank 1
P265D.plain: The position sensor signal for actuator B on bank 1 is above the upper diagnostic threshold. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
causes: Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P265E.title: B Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic Bank 1
P265E.plain: The position sensor signal for actuator B on bank 1 jumps or drops out intermittently. Usually a loose connector or a chafed wire.
causes: Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

P265F.title: Variable A/C Compressor Control Circuit Range/Performance
P265F.plain: The variable-displacement A/C compressor control valve does not respond to commands within tolerance. Refrigerant flow regulation is degraded so cabin temperature varies or efficiency drops.
causes: Control valve spool sticky from oil residue
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

P2660.title: B Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit / Open Bank 2
P2660.plain: The controller cannot drive the rocker arm switching actuator B on bank 2.
causes: Open coil in oil control valve

P2661.title: B Rocker Arm Actuator System Performance/Stuck Off Bank 2
P2661.plain: The rocker arm actuator B on bank 2 is commanded to engage but does not switch.
causes: Low oil pressure cannot move the actuator
Mechanical lock pin stuck in unactivated position
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement

P2662.title: B Rocker Arm Actuator System Stuck On Bank 2
P2662.plain: The rocker arm actuator B on bank 2 stays in the activated state when commanded off.
causes: Mechanical lock pin stuck in activated position
Oil control valve spool stuck open
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement

P2663.title: B Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit Low Bank 2
P2663.plain: Voltage on the rocker arm actuator B control line on bank 2 is below the expected window. Usually a short to ground or a shorted solenoid coil.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2664.title: B Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit High Bank 2
P2664.plain: Voltage on the rocker arm actuator B control line on bank 2 is above the expected window. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open solenoid coil.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2665.title: Fuel Shutoff Valve B Control Circuit / Open
P2665.plain: The controller cannot drive the secondary fuel shutoff valve. Engine cannot be commanded off through this path during a safety event.

P2666.title: Fuel Shutoff Valve B Control Circuit Low
P2666.plain: Voltage on the secondary fuel shutoff valve control line is below the expected window. Usually a short to ground or a shorted solenoid coil.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2667.title: Fuel Shutoff Valve B Control Circuit High
P2667.plain: Voltage on the secondary fuel shutoff valve control line is above the expected window. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open solenoid coil.
causes: Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P2668.title: Fuel Mode Indicator Lamp Control Circuit
P2668.plain: The fuel mode indicator lamp circuit (showing whether a bi-fuel vehicle currently runs on gasoline or alternative fuel) is faulty. Driver may not know the active fuel.
causes: Open or shorted wire to the cluster

P2669.title: Actuator Supply Voltage B Circuit / Open
P2669.plain: The second power feed used to supply actuators (relays, solenoids, motor drivers) is open. All loads on this rail are powerless and report follow-on faults.
causes: Blown fuse on the supply rail
Broken supply wire from main relay

P266A.title: A Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Bank 2
P266A.plain: The position sensor that confirms the A rocker arm switching state on bank 2 returns no usable signal.

P266B.title: A Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance Bank 2
P266B.plain: The position sensor reading does not transition cleanly between the two valve lift modes for actuator A on bank 2.
causes: Sensor signal drift after thermal aging
Worn lock pin reduces travel between modes
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
